value.text: Friends of 18-year-old Kenneth "Kenny" Donahue are mourning the Spanish River High School senior after he was killed in an e-bike crash on West Palmetto Park Road in Boca Raton, just hours after spending Halloween night with friends.Donahue's friends told WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache they are struggling with the sudden loss while remembering the plans they had made together, including attending college.Watch report from Zitlali Solache:A blue cross now marks the area along West Palmetto Park Road where the crash occurred."That's where it happened, so it deserves to be known," said Sawyer Geldert, a close friend of Kenny.The memorial is a place for Donahue's loved ones to remember the 18-year-old they describe as funny, loving, optimistic and caring."I still text him," Geldert said. "It hurts to lose someone so close to you. And if I could see him one last time, I would hug him and never let go."The Boca Raton Police Services Department said its Traffic Homicide Unit is investigating the crash, which happened shortly before 2 a.m. on West Palmetto Park Road between Interstate 95 and Military Trail.According to police, the driver of a 2025 blue Corvette was traveling east on West Palmetto Park Road when the car struck an electric bicycle carrying two people.Police said Donahue was the passenger on the e-bike and suffered fatal injuries. He was pronounced dead at the scene.Police said the 16-year-old operating the e-bike was taken to a hospital and was listed in stable condition. The Corvette driver was not injured.Investigators are evaluating whether criminal charges will be filed in Donahue's death.Friends told WPTV they had spent Halloween night with Donahue before learning hours later that he had been killed."I was speechless," Rafaella Gonzalez said. "I couldn't even feel any emotions in the moment. I was just so devastated."As they grieve, Donahue's friends are focusing on the person they knew."The funny, loving, always optimistic, caring person that you would see every single day," Kazim Raza said.Santiago Rocha said his friend left an impact on those around him."I also feel Kenny was sent from God to teach us about how to love each other," Rocha said.For Donahue's classmates, his absence is especially noticeable at Spanish River High School."I miss being able to give him the hugs I gave him every day," London Adams said. "I miss the way he smelled. I miss the way he laughed. He was genuinely such an important person to all of us. It's really hard for it to be so quiet in school now."Donahue's friends said the loss has also forced them to confront a future they expected him to be part of."We were literally talking about it the night before, where we were going to college together," said Geldert. "I was supposed to dorm with him."Loved ones said Donahue enjoyed sports, working out and spending time with other people. They said he wanted to become a police officer and serve people.Melonie James, who identified herself as a close friend of Donahue's mother, told WPTV that watching his mother grieve has been heartbreaking."She won't get to see her baby graduate," James said.Friends said the 16-year-old who was operating the e-bike is recovering."He's doing well," Hudson Quinonez said. "I'm so glad he's OK because it could've been so much worse."As the investigation continues, Donahue's loved ones are asking anyone who saw what happened to come forward so they can better understand the circumstances surrounding his death."We just need to piece together the night," said James. "We need help."Loved ones have created the email address info@justiceforkenny.com for information about the crash.The Boca Raton Police Services Department is also asking witnesses or anyone with information about the investigation to contact Officer Gonzalez at 561-419-4124. Donahue is expected to be laid to rest Friday.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Lucie County law enforcement officials said they have taken down a major gang following an 18-month investigation.The sheriff's office said the investigation targeted one of Fort Pierce's most violent gangs, which has ties to nearly 100 shootings. Officials are calling the investigation "Operation Scoreboard."WATCH REPORT BELOW: Sheriff Richard Del Toro said members of the 23rd Street Gang kept score of shootings and homicides.Eleven people were arrested Wednesday on racketeering charges, with two warrants still outstanding."We took significant players off the streets yesterday, and there's more to come. There's more operations like this to come because we're not going to tolerate it here in St. Lucie County," Del Toro said Thursday.Investigators said the gang has between 70 and 80 documented members.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. With Democrats poised to take control of both chambers of Congress, attention is quickly turning from the 2026 midterm elections to the leadership battles that will determine who guides the new House and Senate majorities.Leadership elections are expected to begin next week, with Democrats facing some internal pressure over their current leaders and House Republicans preparing for a potentially tight contest of their own.Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries are expected to remain at the top of their respective caucuses. Jeffries would be in position to become House speaker, while Schumer would become Senate majority leader.Both, however, have faced calls from some progressive activists and incoming lawmakers for a change in leadership. Critics argue Democratic leaders did not push back aggressively enough against President Donald Trump while the party was in the minority.RELATED STORY | Democratic leaders outline agenda after sweeping Congress in midtermsAmong those calling for change is Maine Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, who said before Election Day that he would not support Schumer for majority leader."I've already said that I told Senator Schumer that I'm going to support somebody else, so it's no different now," Jackson said.Jackson said he plans to push Democratic leaders on priorities including Medicare for All.House Republicans, meanwhile, face their own leadership battle after Speaker Mike Johnson decided not to seek reelection. Jim Jordan of Ohio, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee and a prominent conservative, is competing against longtime Republican leader Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana.The winner would become one of the highest-profile Republican voices on Capitol Hill as the party moves into the minority.The leadership races come as vote counting continues in two unexpectedly competitive Senate contests in Mississippi and Alaska.In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom holds a narrow lead over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, although neither candidate has reached 50% of the vote. Outstanding absentee, mail and provisional ballots could determine whether either candidate crosses that threshold.In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by fewer than 1,000 votes as counting continues.The outcomes will determine the size of Democrats' Senate majority, but not control of the chamber.Democrats' victories will also create a divided government, with Trump remaining in the White House while Democrats control Congress. That dynamic could create significant hurdles for Democratic priorities.RELATED STORY | Vance blames Iran war for sweeping Republican midterm lossesTrump has threatened to veto Democratic legislation, potentially setting up repeated clashes between the White House and Congress. Democrats have indicated they could use those disputes to build their case ahead of the 2028 elections.Schumer argued this week that Democrats could pass legislation aimed at lowering costs and addressing corruption, forcing Trump to decide whether to sign or veto those measures."If Donald Trump does spend the next year vetoing common sense legislation to lower costs and end corruption, this election, this absolute Republican catastrophe on election night 2026, will look like a good day compared to what will come down on Republicans in the 2028 election," Schumer said.With control of Congress settled but its leadership still taking shape, those internal elections will help determine how Democrats confront Trump and how Republicans position themselves for the next election.

WPTV is working to get answers about how Palm Beach County leaders are responding to historic rainfall that has left neighborhoods underwater, stranded drivers and forced dozens of rescues.The flooding comes during an extraordinary stretch for Palm Beach County, with emergency crews simultaneously responding to flooding, the deadly plane crash near Military Trail and disruptions surrounding Election Day.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Palm Beach County's Emergency Operations Center is operating at Level 2, a partial activation, as county agencies coordinate their response to the flooding and plane crash.Gov. Ron DeSantis expanded Florida's state of emergency Wednesday to include Palm Beach County. The declaration gives state and local officials additional authority and resources for response, recovery and mitigation efforts.County commissioners are now weighing in on the flooding and what they’ve seen in their communities."This rain, my gosh, it never ends," Commissioner Maria Sachs said.Commissioner Gregg Weiss pointed to the extraordinary rainfall totals in parts of West Palm Beach."Parts of West Palm Beach received over 22 inches of rain," Weiss said. "These were epic amounts of water that came down very quickly."Weiss described the rainfall as the kind of extreme event some characterize as a "one-in-1,000-type" storm. He also acknowledged that some residents will be dealing with the consequences long after the rain stops."I know in some of our eastern areas their homes received water inside, so there’s going to be work to do there," Weiss said.For Sachs, the flooding is also raising a larger question about how Palm Beach County prepares for future growth.She pointed to the importance of planning for drainage when new homes and businesses are built."I know our aquifers can take only so much," Sachs said. "When we develop residences and commercial properties, we develop them with the idea of drainage."The flooding has turned roads into waterways, stranded vehicles and left some residents unable to get out of their neighborhoods.Among those who were affected was Commissioner Bobby Powell Jr., who represents Palm Beach County Commission District 7."There's people in my community that were not able to go to work," Powell said.Powell told commissioners that he experienced the flooding firsthand."Fire Rescue came to get me this morning, so I'm one of the people they had to rescue," Powell said.Palm Beach County Fire Rescue told WPTV its crews conducted multiple flood response operations from Sunday through Tuesday.Sunday night, firefighters responded to more than seventy 911 calls in the Century Village area near West Palm Beach. Nearly 100 residents were trapped in stranded vehicles as floodwaters rapidly rose.WATCH BELOW: Flooding in Century VillageFirefighters reported encountering floating cars with people still inside and water reaching between 3 and 4 feet deep in some areas.Crews deployed drones equipped with thermal imaging cameras around Century Village, Cypress Lakes, the Tennis Club and other areas to search vehicles for people who needed help.Firefighters then waded through the water and used high-water vehicles and brush trucks to rescue residents and bring them to higher ground.Fire Rescue said there were no injuries during those operations.Palm Beach County Fire Rescue's Urban Search and Rescue Swiftwater Response Team was also deployed to Riviera Beach for nearly 24 hours.With some streets impassable, rescue specialists used emergency rafts and boats to go door to door.Fire Rescue said its teams:Evacuated 71 peopleConducted two medical rescuesEvacuated nine petsCounty officials have continued reporting significant impacts from the flooding in Riviera Beach and other communities.PBCFR said from Nov. 1-3, crews responded to a total of more than 1,600 emergency calls across the county. This figure included all 911 calls, not just flooding.The flooding wasn't the only major emergency stretching Palm Beach County's resources.At the same time, fire rescue crews were carrying out flood response operations; dozens of personnel and resources were also dedicated to the deadly Learjet crash near Greenacres.The crash also displaced an estimated 400 to 600 people from a nearby mobile home community. WPTV spoke with residents who were unable to return to their homes, vehicles and belongings while investigators worked through the crash scene.The county then opened an emergency shelter where some residents have been ever since."We've been communicating with our municipalities, making sure we have shelters, that we have anything needed to address the concerns of our families," said Commissioner Joel Flores, adding Election Day presented another challenge as he noted three precincts had to be moved because of all the flooding.Vice Mayor Marci Woodward pointed to the strain of responding to both disasters at once."We had a horrific plane crash and also ended up with flooding, so to all the employees that have worked a lot of long hours, I wanted to personally thank all of you, and I know our residents appreciate all the efforts, so thank you for that," Woodward said.State of emergency now includes Palm Beach CountyThe county’s response is continuing with the state now involved in recovery efforts.DeSantis amended Florida's existing flooding emergency order Wednesday to add Palm Beach County along with Glades, Hendry, Lake, Okeechobee, Seminole and Volusia counties.The Florida Division of Emergency Management said the move strengthens the state's ability to deploy resources, support local response efforts and help communities recover.The emergency declaration also gives state and local officials additional authority to carry out response, recovery and mitigation efforts, including logistical, rescue and evacuation operations. Local governments can waive certain procedures involving public works, contracts, equipment, workers and spending when necessary to speed up the emergency response.If you're in need of flooding emergency, call 2-1-1.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The passing of Amendment 3 has now put Florida cities on notice to find ways to handle the anticipated loss of revenue."I was interviewed a couple of years ago when this first came up, and I said, 'What are we going to do, have a bake sale,' and here we are," says Lake Worth Beach Mayor Betty Resch.WATCH REPORT BELOW: According to Florida Tax Watch, Lake Worth Beach stands to lose $2.9 million in the first year of the higher homestead exemption and $5 million in the second year."We can't just keep raising the fees. We can't charge somebody if they want to go to the library," Resch said.Voters made a statement on affordability, with 62% approving the referendum. The measure raises the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, which will mean savings on property tax bills.Local governments that depend on property tax revenue now face tightening budgets by making cuts, reducing services and possibly finding new ways to raise revenue."We don't charge yet for parking downtown, and every time we talk about it, everybody flips out because they don't want it and neither do I," Resch said. "I don't know where we're going to go. I don't know what we're going to do."

Investigators have recovered a portion of an engine from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres on Sunday as crews continue excavating the crash site, according to the National Transportation Safety Board.The NTSB said excavation work began late Wednesday and continued Thursday as investigators and local officials worked to recover wreckage from the crash that killed nine people.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Part of jet's engine found, NTSB saysDebris from the aircraft has been found away from the main impact site, including on the roofs of nearby homes and buildings, according to the NTSB. All recovered wreckage will be taken to a secure location for further examination.Investigators are also asking residents who find debris believed to be from the Learjet not to keep it or attempt to move, alter or dispose of it.WATCH BELOW: Piece of jet's tail found miles away The agency said even small pieces of wreckage could contain evidence that helps investigators determine what happened.Anyone who has found or collected debris from the crash is asked to email witness@ntsb.gov to arrange for its recovery. The NTSB is asking people to include a photograph of the debris in the email, if possible.The NTSB said recovering as much of the aircraft wreckage as possible is critical to its investigation and efforts to determine the cause of the crash.

Days after heavy rain moved through the area, floodwaters are still creating problems for local farms and nurseries, forcing some to close to visitors and adding to months of weather-related challenges.WPTV reporter Christy Waite visited Happy Place Ranch in Palm City, where standing water surrounds much of the property as the owners work to recover from the flooding.WATCH REPORT BELOW: For owner Amanda Cimorelli, seeing the ranch underwater has been emotional."It's crushing," Cimorelli said as she fought back tears. "It's sad."She said they expected rain, but not the amount that ultimately fell."We figured it was just rain. It was relentless," she said.For seven years, Happy Place Ranch has hosted horse shows, riding lessons, birthday parties and other activities. Now, the flooding has forced the ranch to close, costing the business money while adding new expenses.Cimorelli said the ranch has been losing revenue since October as weather forced it to cancel activities, including its fall festival and horse shows.The flooding could now force the ranch to cancel two upcoming birthday parties, something Cimorelli said has never happened in the seven years they have been there."It's just thousands and thousands of dollars of revenue lost and extra cash going out that we really don't have right now," she said.One of those added expenses is hay. With the flooding affecting the property, the ranch is spending more money to make sure its animals have what they need.Despite the flooding, Cimorelli said all of the animals are OK. The challenge is finding enough dry space for them."I have nowhere to put farm animals. We got everyone in the barn as much as we can," she said.For now, the ranch is focused on cleaning up and waiting for the water to recede."All we can do is wait," Cimorelli said. "Just wait and figure it out day by day."Meanwhile, in Loxahatchee Groves, Gardino Nursery is also dealing with flooding after an already difficult year of weather extremes.Owner Sid Gardino said the nursery has endured a freeze, drought and now excess water."The freeze was probably the worst we have experienced," Gardino said. "Then the drought came, and I prayed for rain. I think I prayed too hard because now we have all of this."Water reached shin level in some areas, while thick mud made it difficult to walk around the property."It's frustrating. It's hard to walk with this much rain. We are working at 20% capacity," Gardino said.Gardino Nursery operates by appointment only. The nursery said it is still able to ship products, but customers currently cannot visit the property to see plants in person.The business does not yet know how much revenue has been lost because of the flooding.There is some encouraging news. Gardino said the property is already beginning to recover. They hope that if the sunny and warm weather continues, they can be back open by next week.

Washington Elementary School in Palm Beach County will remain closed Friday as severe flooding and dangerous conditions continue to affect parts of the community, according to the school district.All other schools operated by the School District of Palm Beach County will be open Friday, Chief of Communications Sean Cooley said.The district said its priority is reopening schools only when it is safe to do so, acknowledging that some neighborhoods continue to experience severe flooding that could make travel difficult or dangerous.Families and staff members who cannot safely get to school are being urged not to put themselves at risk. Any student absences caused by weather-related impacts will be fully excused through Friday, according to the district."Our top priority is reopening schools only when it is safe to do so," the district said. "We recognize that several of our neighborhoods are still dealing with severe flooding and dangerous conditions."The district also thanked teachers, bus drivers, school leaders, custodians and other staff members who helped reopen schools following the severe weather."We appreciate the flexibility, patience, and understanding as we've worked through these severe weather conditions and flooding," the district said.All public schools in St. Lucie and Indian River counties will be closed Friday.

Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation’s second-largest city.The India-born Raman's upstart campaign marked a generational shift at City Hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year. Raman, though, never attracted the same level of national attention and stressed her willingness to break with the progressive party at times during the campaign.Her entry into the race marked a stunning change of heart after she had initially endorsed Bass, once her ally. She said the city had reached a “breaking point” and announced her own candidacy just before the filing deadline.Bass said in a statement that she called Raman to congratulate her on her victory.“While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,” Bass said. “I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a bid for reelection. Her first term was undone by the deadly Palisades Fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. The devastation left many voters with the unshakeable feeling that Bass should be held to account, and she never recovered.Raman's rise came in a year that saw Democratic divisions across the country, with insurgent left-wing candidates challenging establishment rivals.Raman is promising to oust the police chief, whom she views as too accommodating with federal immigration authorities. She also wants to improve basic services that have deteriorated for years and left neighborhoods with dirty, pothole-ridden streets, buckled sidewalks and broken streetlights.Raman called Bass’ efforts to reduce homelessness ineffective. She's promising a new approach on the crisis that would expand medical teams for people who live in encampments and on the streets in an effort to build trust and eventually bring them indoors. Raman also wants to provide more housing to move people out of hotels rented by the city for those who are homeless.She said her plans could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when the city will host the Olympic Games. However, the problem has long proved intractable, despite billions spent in the region.RELATED STORY | Keisha Lance Bottoms to become Georgia’s first Black governor, first woman governorRaman offered changeRaman, 45, was the face of change in a year when voters were restless over long-running problems that persisted under Bass, 73. A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted from Oct. 19 to 25 found that about 4 in 10 likely voters said reducing the number of homeless encampments should be a top priority for the next mayor to address, while about 3 in 10 said that about ensuring public safety or building more affordable housing.She was able to overcome criticism from Bass that she was “not ready for primetime” and too inexperienced to run a city with 3.8 million people, and she capitalized on anxiety over the future.“Our city is in crisis,” she said in one ad. The ad showed a lectern with no one behind it at the site of a massive warehouse fire from last summer, the homeless epicenter of Skid Row and shuttered malls and storefronts. “Where is our mayor?” Raman asked.Bass argued that she made enough progress to merit a second four-year term, and she branded Raman’s views on policing and homelessness as “extreme.”RELATED STORY | Xavier Becerra wins California gubernatorial race, making history as the state’s second Latino leaderTop Democrats lined up with BassRaman's victory came despite limited backing from the Democratic establishment. Bass had support from Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with nearly every member of the City Council. Bass served in the state Legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022 and was under consideration to be former President Joe Biden’s running mate in 2020.In an important signal to the business community, billionaire developer Rick Caruso said he was voting for Bass, but stopped short of formally endorsing the candidate he lost to in the 2022 mayoral race.Raman, an urban planner, picked up notable support from advocacy and political groups, including Our Revolution, which was founded by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. But she was thin on endorsements from prominent local politicians.She landed a widely publicized private meeting with former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, who was not involved in the race, that hinted at her efforts to broaden her circle. Expanding her network of allies could be crucial as she begins governing a city that's home to a struggling entertainment industry, a major port, world-class universities and research institutions and serves as a major tourist destination.

Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off.St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update, saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help."If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies," Del Toro said.Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff.WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power & Light's equipment remains underwater."We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else," FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. "Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety."Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment.Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high.Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede.Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

Public schools in Indian River and St. Lucie counties will remain closed Friday, Nov. 6, with both districts planning to reopen Monday, Nov. 9, as flooding continues to affect transportation and access to some campuses. In Indian River County, the school district cited limited bus driver availability and significant delays along County Roads 510 and 512. School buildings will be accessible to instructional staff preparing for Monday’s return. Activities and extracurriculars are scheduled to resume Thursday, Nov. Additionally, the Palm Beach County School District announced that Washington Elementary School will remain closed Friday. Lucie County, the district said flooding has left some bus stops and roads inaccessible and affected access to some campuses. Some families and employees also remain without power or cannot safely leave their neighborhoods. Lucie Public Schools canceled athletics through Sunday, Nov. Athletic activities may resume Monday. The SAT scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, has been rescheduled for Nov. See also: 'Up to my chest': Family raises concerns after 7-year-old walks through deep floodwaters Five Boys & Girls Clubs locations in St. Lucie County will be open from 8 a.m. for current members and anyone interested in joining. Each site can accommodate up to 100 members, who may attend any location. Families can register at bgcofslc.org . Children should bring a packed lunch, snack and water bottle. The locations are: Chuck Hill, 198 Marion Ave., Port St. Jenkins Road, Fort Pierce Ken Pruitt, 10673 SE Lennard Road, Port St. Lucie Percy Peek Teen, 2902 Avenue D, Fort Pierce Garden Terrace, 3104 Avenue J, Fort Pierce The St. Lucie County district said it will share information about any required instructional make-up days when available. Both districts said they will continue monitoring conditions and sharing updates through their official channels.

Elon Musk spent more money on the 2026 midterm elections than any political donor in American history. In Texas, the state his companies call home, it didn't buy him the results he wanted.The world's richest man spent at least $474 million on the midterms, including about $224 million in Texas, according to campaign finance records. On Tuesday, Texas voters elected Democrat James Talarico to the U.S. Senate over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, the candidate Musk spent the most to support. They also ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in favor of Democrat Gina Hinojosa.RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governorThe biggest share of Musk's Texas spending moved in two checks in September. According to the Senate Leadership Fund's third-quarter Federal Election Commission report, Musk gave the main Senate Republican super PAC $75 million on Sept. 9 and another $83 million on Sept. 23.The day after each donation, the fund transferred the exact same amount to Texas PAC, a super PAC supporting Paxton. The filings don't prove Musk's specific dollars funded those transfers, but the timing drew wide attention.Musk also gave Abbott $5 million in the final stretch of the race, according to state campaign finance filings first reported by Politico. The $474 million total runs only through mid-October. Post-election FEC reports due Dec. 3 will show whether he gave more in the campaign's final weeks.For Musk, the spending is a small slice of his fortune. With a net worth estimated at roughly $875 billion, the $474 million amounts to about 0.05% of his wealth. That's roughly the equivalent of someone with $400,000 to their name spending $200, according to a Scripps News calculation.Texas has become the home base for Musk's business empire. He began moving operations there in 2020 after clashing with California over pandemic restrictions at Tesla's factory in the state.Today, Tesla runs its largest U.S. vehicle factory outside Austin, and SpaceX launches rockets from its Starbase complex in South Texas. In August, SpaceX and Tesla picked Grimes County for Terafab, a chip manufacturing complex projected to cost $55 billion in its first phase and up to $119 billion in total.Those operations rely heavily on state decisions about electricity, water, environmental permits, infrastructure and tax incentives. Abbott had been a vocal supporter of Musk's projects, and Paxton's office had largely avoided scrutinizing Musk's companies even as it took on other Big Tech firms.Talarico made the flood of outside money part of his message on election night."We went up against all the negative ads, smear campaigns, foreign bots, and AI deepfakes that money can buy," Talarico said. "They played dirty because they were desperate. And against big money and long odds, we took our power back."IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Trump deflects blame for Republican midterm losses as finger-pointing beginsInvestors reacted quickly. SpaceX shares closed down 3.8% on Wednesday and Tesla fell 3.3%, even as the broader market rose, and are tracking even further drops during market trading Thursday.Musk responded on X with a nod to one of his newer ventures: "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now."Hinojosa inherits the office that oversaw more than $1.6 billion in tax incentives for Musk's companies. She campaigned against generous corporate subsidies and has promised to freeze new data center approvals until the Legislature puts protections in place.Her campaign has said Terafab alone received about $1.7 billion in school tax exemptions. The governor's office also controls the Texas Enterprise Fund, which gave SpaceX $30 million for the project. Tesla is separately seeking state incentives for a proposed $10 billion solar cell plant near Houston.Those incentives matter beyond Musk's balance sheet. When a state grants a company a tax break, that's revenue it doesn't collect, and the cost is typically absorbed by other taxpayers or reflected in public budgets.Hinojosa's win doesn't cancel existing agreements or stop Musk's companies from operating in Texas. But her administration could take a tougher approach to permitting and new incentives as his companies look to expand.Musk also faces a new landscape in Washington, where Democrats will control both the House and Senate in January. Even with President Donald Trump holding veto power, congressional Democrats can issue subpoenas without his signature.

Lucie and Indian River counties will remain closed Friday, Nov. 6, as flooding continues to make some roads, bus stops and school campuses difficult or unsafe to access.Both school districts said they expect schools to reopen Monday, Nov. 9.WATCH REPORT BELOW:While conditions have improved in parts of St. Lucie County, district officials said a significant number of bus stops and roads remain inaccessible because of flooding. Access to some campuses also continues to be affected.The district said some families and employees remain without power or cannot safely leave their neighborhoods."Conditions vary greatly across our county," the St. Lucie Public Schools District said in its announcement. "Although some neighborhoods have returned to normal, others continue to experience flooding that makes traveling to school, whether on foot, by bus, or by car, unsafe."All St. Lucie Public Schools athletic activities are canceled through Sunday, Nov. A nearly two-year investigation into the 23rd Street gang has led to nearly 40 arrests and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash, law enforcement officials said Thursday. The multi-agency investigation, called Operation Score Board, focused on alleged gang activity in northwest Fort Pierce and surrounding areas. Officials said investigators linked 13 people to an alleged criminal conspiracy involving fraud, drug trafficking, shootings and homicides. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said investigators reviewed 10 years of criminal activity and connected people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings. Investigators also found that gang members allegedly kept a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, which inspired the operation’s name. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said local, state and federal agencies took part in the investigation. The sheriff’s office, F ort Pierce Police Department , ATF , FBI , DEA , Florida Department of Law Enforcement , U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations were among the participating agencies. "Hundreds of shootings over the last decade, violent crime terrorizing the north end of this county, and our community deserves better, and they're getting better because of the hard work of the men and women with the special investigation units that the chief mentioned, and our federal partners here," said Sheriff Richard Del Toro. Officials said about 70 to 80 people are documented as members of the gang. The investigation focused on people police described as shot callers who allegedly directed its activities. Authorities said the 23rd Street gang has been a problem in the Fort Pierce area for decades and was the most violent of several gangs in the city. 4, officers served five search warrants four in Fort Pierce and one in Port St. Lucie beginning around 5 a.m. The operation led to 11 arrests on racketeering charges, with two people still wanted on warrants, and four additional probable-cause arrests, officials said. Authorities said some people connected to the investigation had already been arrested during its earlier stages. 4 searches yielded seven firearms, about one pound of marijuana, 15 grams of cocaine, 50 grams of MDMA and $18,474. Across the investigation, police said they seized 18 firearms, 20 pounds of marijuana, 532 grams of cocaine and two grams of MDPV. "We remain committed to identifying, investigating, and holding accountable those responsible for bringing violence and criminal activity into our neighborhoods," Chief Smith said. "Our message is clear: We will not tolerate organized criminal activity that threatens the safety of our residents." Authorities did not identify the people they believe led the gang, but said they believe they have arrested most of the key players. They said some people connected to the investigation have faced murder charges, but declined to discuss active cases. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro called the operation an unusually large collaboration among local, state and federal agencies. He said investigators took significant players off the streets and that more operations are expected. The sheriff said the case took extensive work to connect years of records and evidence, and involved a 2,000-page report and a 150-page affidavit. Officials also credited the State Attorney’s Office with helping build the case. History of problems CBS12 previously reported on gang violence in the region, including a 2022 ride-along with St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office gang intelligence unit Detective Solomon Archie. Archie said Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street and 29th Street gangs operated on opposite sides of the area divided by 25th Street and Martin Luther King Jr. He also described gun violence as a major concern and said law enforcement agencies were working across county lines to identify suspects and respond to crime. In 2017, CBS12 also reported that the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office had launched a six-month crackdown on gangs and drugs in Fort Pierce. At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized.

Law enforcement officials in St. Lucie County announced Thursday that 40 suspected members of a Fort Pierce gang have been arrested following an 18-month investigation. The investigation, known as "Operation Score Board," targeted the 23rd Street Gang, which authorities say has operated in northern St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the gang has between 70 and 80 members and has been responsible for years of violence in the Fort Pierce community. "This gang has terrorized, basically created a hostage crisis for our community up there," Del Toro said. "There’s a lot of good people that are up there in Fort Pierce that have been just held hostage by this group for the last decade, living in fear." Investigators said the gang even maintained a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, a discovery that ultimately gave the operation its name. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said detectives reviewed a decade of criminal activity to identify connections between suspected gang members and violent crimes. "Detectives conducted an extensive review of criminal activity spanning ten years, examining incidents and identifying connections between individuals associated with the gang," Smith said. "This intensive analysis revealed a disturbing pattern of organized crime and violence." Authorities said investigators used Florida’s RICO law to connect years of alleged shootings, drug trafficking and other criminal activity to members of the 23rd Street Gang. The investigation involved multiple local and state law enforcement agencies working together over 18 months to build cases against suspected members of the organization. On Wednesday, law enforcement officers executed multiple search warrants throughout the Fort Pierce area, resulting in 11 arrests as part of the larger operation. Authorities said officers also seized multiple firearms, drugs and thousands of dollars in cash. Del Toro said the size of the operation and the cooperation between agencies could have a lasting impact on the community. "I’ve never seen an operation this large with this many agencies at the local and federal level," Del Toro said. "I think this is going to have a significant generational impact in this community." Authorities said similar investigations and operations are expected in the future. A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago. Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WFLX that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense’s second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. Camerlengo’s attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense’s amended motion was “procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.” Wednesday’s ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set. Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Her arrest followed a WFLX investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade. The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case. During a contentious July hearing , Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo’s defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial. “I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,” Metzger said. “This case has been continued so many times, I’ve lost count.” In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial. Camerlengo’s defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths. “I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don’t think she had all of the facts,” Kaplan previously told WFLX. Among those closely following the case is Adele Kirk Csontos, whose dog, Mako, died after spending approximately 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022. Kirk Csontos filed a police report following Mako’s death, but Camerlengo was never charged in connection with it because his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs determined they died from blunt force trauma, leading to Camerlengo’s arrest. “I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn’t think it would be two years,” Kirk Csontos previously told WFLX. Despite the repeated delays, she said she remains hopeful. Believe it or not, I’m still hopeful that she will be held accountable,” she said. Camerlengo’s next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. No trial date has been announced.

Palm Beach County students are helping scientists answer a deceptively simple question: Where does our trash go once it starts floating through local waterways?ANGARI Foundation plans to release bright orange, eco-friendly drift cards into the water on Nov. 10 at noon as part of its Lagoon Drift Card Study. Members of the public are then being asked to find the cards and report where they ended up.“So we're basically trying to track our trash,” Laura Jessop with ANGARI Foundation told WPTV. “So we put these eco-friendly drift cards in the water. They're going in on November 10 at 12 p.m., and we need the public to go out and find them.”The idea is to use the cards as stand-ins for other objects floating on the surface.“Everything that floats on the surface, that's what we're sort of tracking right now,” Jessop said.Each card found by a member of the public becomes another piece of information for the study.Jessop said knowing where the cards eventually turn up can help researchers identify places where floating debris could be accumulating.“They're bright orange, and if they report them to us, we can then look at where our trash is accumulating and really target those areas,” she said.The project involves Manatee Lagoon, where some of the drift cards will be released.Rachel Shanker with Manatee Lagoon said participating in the project can provide information that may ultimately help protect Florida's environment.“Here at Manatee Lagoon, we're so excited to be a part of this study where we can collect data and learn how to better preserve and protect Florida's environment and wildlife for future generations,” Shanker said.The study isn't limited to scientists and environmental organizations.Students from Palm Springs Community Middle School are creating their own drift cards and will release them at Manatee Lagoon on Nov. 10.A teacher participating in the project told WPTV the experiment gives students the opportunity to connect what they're studying in class with an actual environmental project.“My students are creating drift cards which they will be releasing on November 10 here at Manatee Lagoon, and they are doing this to track the pollution in the waterways and apply what we're learning in the classroom to the real world,” she said.And the students aren't sending anonymous pieces of orange material into the water.They're making the cards their own.One student decorated a card with water, a sun and a shark, before adding a marine-themed message: “You're 'fintastic.'”Another decorated a card as an ocean scene with a simple message for whoever eventually discovers it: “Love your ocean.”For students, the cards turn an environmental lesson into something tangible.They create the cards, release them, and wait to see where currents carry them. If members of the public find and report their locations, those discoveries become part of the study.That provides a real-world demonstration of something that can otherwise be difficult to visualize in a classroom: What happens to floating material after it enters a waterway?For the broader community, it also turns a walk along the water into an opportunity to participate in local science.If you spot one of the bright orange drift cards, it may be more than something that washed ashore. Its location is precisely the information researchers are looking for.The experiment comes just before another important date for the Lake Worth Lagoon.Manatee season officially begins Nov. 15.Shanker said cooler temperatures help bring manatees back toward Manatee Lagoon.“As the water temperatures drop, they start coming here to Manatee Lagoon for our warm water outflow,” Shanker said.Manatee Lagoon plans to celebrate the beginning of the season with a kickoff event Nov. 21.For the students creating drift cards, meanwhile, the next milestone comes Nov. 10, when their colorful creations leave their hands and begin their journey through South Florida's waterways.Where they end up is part of the experiment.Who finds them could be anyone.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Blue Repose Foundation is launching a pilot program designed to help law enforcement officers and other public safety professionals recover from occupational stress through weekly float sessions, peer support and coping techniques.The startup nonprofit introduced the program at Float8 in Delray Beach, where Blue Repose Founder and President Bridget Coghlan discussed the pressures public safety professionals can encounter and the stigma that may prevent some from seeking support.“With our field, of course, we're exposed to traumas, long shift hours, and things of that nature,” Coghlan said. “We don't like to say mental health, so we just want to take care of the person and give them resources to do so within their professional life and their personal life at home.”Coghlan said the pilot will include five participants during its initial monthlong run at Transitions Wellness and Performance Center in Juno Beach.“They'll get a float session, one per week, followed by peer support and other coping decompression techniques to follow and hopefully it'll help them out,” Coghlan said.The program is part of Blue Repose Foundation’s developing mission to provide private, nonclinical restorative opportunities to law enforcement officers, corrections professionals and others working in public safety.Blue Repose says the foundation is being established in Martin County, with an initial focus on serving the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County. Kristen Neves, the foundation’s director of community engagement and partnerships, said Blue Repose is seeking financial support to launch the pilot.“We're really looking for the community support right now to fund this program and get this pilot program up and going,” Neves said. “We just really want to get this out there and get those law enforcement supported.”Information about contributing to the program is available on the Blue Repose Foundation website.Float8 owner Matt Beck said the Delray Beach studio uses float cabins rather than pods.Float cabins contain shallow water with a high concentration of Epsom salt, allowing a person to remain buoyant. The private environment also reduces outside light, sound and other stimulation.“By reducing the effects of gravity and external stimulation on the body, it helps induce a meditative state, downregulate your nervous system, and help you recover from those stressful situations that our law enforcement officers face so often,” Beck said.Blue Repose describes the float experience as one component of a broader program that will include peer support and additional coping and decompression techniques.Public safety professionals can encounter trauma, long shifts, and sustained stress while serving their communities. Blue Repose’s pilot reflects an effort to give participants structured time to decompress while connecting them with support beyond the float cabin.The initial program will allow Blue Repose to begin evaluating its approach with a small group of participants as the nonprofit works to secure community funding.The foundation’s broader goal is to help professionals take care of themselves in both their working and personal lives while making recovery a more accepted part of public service.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. After noticing worsening water quality while rowing, South Fork High School senior Bianca Bernhard founded the Martin Oyster Restoration Initiative (MORI) a student-led nonprofit that recycles oyster shells to support restoration projects in local waterways.“The water quality got really bad,” Bernhard told WPTV’s T.A. “That’s due to discharges from Lake Okeechobee, so I decided to do something with the extra free time.”The initiative, known as MORI, collects oyster shells from local restaurants. Volunteers at South Fork High School then help dry and cure the shells so they can be used in restoration projects.WATCH: Stuart student leads oyster restoration mission“I recycle a lot of shells from local restaurants,” Bernhard said. “These local shells will help create new reef structures like what I’m holding right here, and those reef structures will grow new oysters which will filter the water.”South Fork High School students and teachers have joined Bernhard’s conservation effort through the school’s marine science, construction and agriculture programs.During the WPTV segment, Jennifer Inostroza, a teacher at South Fork High School, explained that the school helps cure and dry the oyster shells so they are ready for future projects.Information provided by the Martin County School District says MORI has recruited more than 60 students and teachers and amassed approximately 1,600 pounds of oyster shell.The district says participating students can earn honor credits through South Fork High School’s Marine Sciences program.The recycled shells do not immediately return to the water. They must first be transported, dried and cured before they can be incorporated into approved restoration structures.According to Bernhard, those structures provide places where new oysters can grow. She said the oysters then help filter and clean the surrounding water.MORI is also collaborating with Docks for a Clean Lagoon, a nonprofit that installs vertical oyster gardens. According to Bernhard’s Go Blue Awards narrative, shells cured by South Fork volunteers have been used in the creation of vertical oyster gardens intended for the Indian River Lagoon.Bernhard is a finalist in the Blue Hatchling Youth category of Loggerhead Marinelife Center’s 2026 Go Blue Awards.“Bianca is one of our finalists for the Go Blue Hatchling Awards,” said Audrey Padgett, VP of Marketing, at Loggerhead Marinelife Center, told WPTV. “We’ve had nominees from all over the world. So it’s really amazing to see someone selected by this independent panel of judges here in our backyard for the work that she’s doing to improve ocean conservation and ecosystems right here.”The annual awards recognize young people, individuals, businesses and nonprofit organizations making contributions to ocean conservation.The 2026 Go Blue Awards ceremony is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. 30, at the Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach.Bernhard’s work comes as MORI prepares for its next phase. According to her Go Blue Awards narrative, she aims to expand the initiative to three additional local schools during the 2026-27 school year.She also plans to pursue oyster restoration research with the Florida Oceanographic Society and work with students to develop additional structures for restoration projects.For Bernhard, the project began with something she saw while rowing. It has since grown into a broader effort that gives students a hands-on role in responding to the environmental challenges facing their community.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Thomas Wayne Markle, the father of Meghan Markle, was arrested Friday in Florida on a federal charge of possessing child pornography after investigators said they found suspected child sexual abuse material in two Los Angeles-area storage units he had rented for nearly two decades.The 82-year-old Lakeland resident is charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to federal prosecutors. He was expected to make his initial appearance Friday in federal court in Tampa.The FBI investigation began after authorities learned in October that a person had signed an affidavit describing the discovery of suspected child sexual abuse material among Thomas Markle's belongings in the Philippines, according to an affidavit filed with the criminal complaint.Investigators later learned Thomas Markle rented a storage unit in the Los Angeles area. Information provided by the person who reported the material in the Philippines eventually led authorities to a second storage unit, according to the affidavit.Federal agents obtained search warrants for both units, which investigators said Thomas Markle had rented since 2008. According to prosecutors, his most recent payments for the units were made through automatic payments last month.During searches of the units, FBI agents seized roughly 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books containing suspected child sexual abuse material, according to the news release.Federal authorities allege some of the photographs show an adult man, identified by a witness as Thomas Markle, with prepubescent girls. Investigators said other photographs appeared to depict Markle with children in various stages of undress."These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.FBI officials said the case demonstrates the importance of reporting suspected child exploitation to law enforcement."This case highlights the importance of the involvement of the public, even if it's a family member or close friend, to be vigilant and speak up if they have information on individuals they suspect may be preying on and exploiting our children," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office, said.Thomas Markle is the estranged father of Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex and wife of Prince Harry.The FBI is investigating the case. If convicted, Thomas Markle faces a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.His arrest follows reports by The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghan's half-brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out the home of their father in the Philippines.Meghan recently said she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to London police in 2018."It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. "I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits,” married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.Thomas Markle Sr. was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr. recently found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s former home in Cebu City, in the Philippines, when he was clearing out the property.Markle Jr. told the newspaper that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI."I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him."

Floodwaters continue to inundate properties in Martin County, leaving cattle farmers struggling to care for their animals and residents concerned about how much longer the water will remain. Residents in the Trailside community say water from neighboring properties is flowing into their drainage system, causing widespread flooding. Flooding threatens cattle, farm operations Hungryland Farms normally operates a 20-acre rotational grazing system for its Florida Cracker cattle. The owner, Melissa, said much of the pasture is now underwater, forcing the animals onto the farm’s elevated driveway. "We're starting to lose big sections of the driveway. We have them concentrated up the house pad, but if we lose too much more, we're just going to have to figure out a way to evacuate them somewhere," she said. Some cattle have struggled to navigate the water, and Melissa said the farm is concerned about losing access to its property as flooding continues. For now, the farm is bringing in hay and hay cubes to keep the cattle on their regular diet while monitoring potential health risks from floodwaters. "We’re more just concerned with the health and safety of our cattle," Melissa said. Melissa said the farm has an emergency contact with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service if the animals face imminent danger. "We don’t know how long we’re going to be here," she said. HOA says solution is unclear Kyla Shay, president of the Trailside Homeowners Association, said the community’s drainage system is designed to handle water from its 41 lots and designated neighboring properties. However, Shay said water from outside that system is now flowing through county-owned land and other neighboring properties before reaching the community’s southern canal. We can’t handle theirs," Shay said. The flooding has also affected neighboring pastures and reached areas near Bridge Road and an electrical substation, according to Shay. She said some electrical transformers are partially underwater, septic systems are overwhelmed and residents have been warned their well water could be compromised. "The health department issued warnings this morning to me that our water wells could be compromised because of bacteria, because of the standing water," Shay said. Since their septic systems are submerged, Shay said homeowners have been unable to shower or do laundry. County says repairs must wait WPBF 25 News reached out to Martin County about their concerns and learned the county recently acquired approximately 315 acres of land in the area, known as the Elise J. A county spokesperson said establishing access has been their immediate priority so staff can assess conditions and respond. The county said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District to address a breach affecting drainage into its irrigation canal and that the agencies jointly determined repairs should wait until water levels recede. The county said current conditions make hauling and placing sand unsafe and potentially damaging to the levee. Material could also wash into the canal before crews establish a stable repair. "County staff will continue to monitor water levels and site conditions in close coordination with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District," a county spokesperson said. The county said it will move forward with repairs when conditions allow safe work without compromising the levee. It is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce the risk of flooding happening again. Residents want a long-term solution Shay said the homeowners association has been working with water engineers and other experts to understand how long the flooding could last. "It's probably going to be late January, February before we can see a break, and that's assuming that the south canal wall does not collapse and immediately dump all the water on us," she said. Melissa said the farm’s drainage system normally provides room for water to collect during the rainy season, but the amount coming from outside the property has overwhelmed it. "We have a very extensive drainage system, but it’s just not equipped to handle this amount of water," Melissa said. Both women said they want neighboring properties and the agencies responsible for drainage to address the problem. For now, Martin County said it will continue monitoring conditions and coordinating with the conservancy district before attempting repairs. Meanwhile, Melissa said the farm is focused on keeping its cattle safe as water continues to surround the property.

Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help."If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies," Del Toro said.Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff.WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power & Light's equipment remains underwater."We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else," FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. "Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety."Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment.Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high.Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede.Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

Much of a Jensen Beach neighborhood on Hyline Drive is underwater after this week's heavy rain overwhelmed the local drainage system. As of Wednesday afternoon, water levels inside some homes are still rising long after the rain stopped.For Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid, a kayak has become the way to get around their flooded community.WATCH REPORT BELOW: At Kincaid's home, the water level is waist-deep."We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can," said Kincaid.At French's home, the damage has just begun, with the water level climbing to 4 inches deep."My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else," French said.Their homes are among dozens in the neighborhood under water after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and inundated the drainage system."We were expecting flooding to go down. Clearly drainage is not — things are not draining correctly," Kincaid said.Martin County told us the neighborhood is uniquely located next to the Savannas Preserve, where water is naturally flowing south from other areas that flooded. For now, the county says it's unable to pump water out of the community because the nearby watershed doesn't have capacity, but relief may be on the horizon."As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that," Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said. "We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction."Residents are hoping relief comes sooner rather than later so they can start the long road to recovery."Even after, like, our houses are wrecked," French said."It's just a lot to take in right now for us," Kincaid said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie police are evacuating residents from the flooded Vitalia community as dangerous waters continue to affect neighborhoods more than 48 hours into the flooding emergency. I think it's part of living in Florida," said Sheri George, a Vitalia resident. Sheri George and her husband Arthur were evacuated by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission on a swamp buggy Wednesday. They had no electricity, no A/C and the food in their refrigerator was spoiling. They were unable to drive out of the neighborhood because roads were flooded. They were thrilled FWC could get them safely out of the neighborhood. This is definitely, whoever's idea this was, thank you. 'Cause otherwise we would've been stuck there, who knows how much longer," Sheri George said. "I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me," said Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident who was evacuated because of flooding. According to FWC, since Tuesday they've evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater in several areas in St. "I love being able to, when we're at our worst times being able to come and give somebody some ray of hope," said Jon Arnold, an FWC investigator who was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia. "I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety," said Tyson Matthews, FWC Public Information Officer. Lucie Police Department said officers and emergency personnel were helping residents affected by ongoing flooding get to safety. The department urged people to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads. In Valencia Cay at Riverland, some residents told CBS12 they were effectively trapped in their homes and unable to get their cars out of their driveways because of flooded streets. Some said water reached their garages but did not enter their homes. CBS12 also observed water 18 inches deep in the street. See also: Two injured, third person believed dead after helicopter crash near Key Biscayne The flooding has continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain has moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly. Lucie received 16.7 inches of rain from Nov. Lucie County received between 7 and 17 inches during that period, according to the National Weather Service. Residents told CBS12 the flooding was the worst they had seen in their neighborhood. Police urged residents to never drive or walk through floodwaters, follow evacuation instructions, stay away from closed roads and check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones if they can do so safely. As of Wednesday evening, the St. Lucie County Fire District says it has responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents countywide. In the Vitalia community, the City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department has installed a 12-inch pump, which began operating at approximately 8:00 p.m. tonight, the fire district said. The pump is moving an estimated 7,000 8,000 gallons of water per minute to help reduce flooding in the neighborhood. Additionally, SLCFD says routine evacuation operations in Vitalia have been suspended overnight and are scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Emergency responders remain available for fire and medical emergencies. Residents experiencing immediate safety or serious medical concerns requiring assistance should call 911.

A viral video showing a student swimming home from a school bus in flooded Port St. Lucie streets has raised questions about why schools opened during Monday’s severe weather. The video, filmed in a neighborhood where water has since receded, shows the student navigating deep floodwaters after exiting the bus. "He literally almost went completely underwater," said Lucinda Lopez, a Port St. Another neighbor, Ariel Abel, described the scene: "We watched the school bus get stuck over in that turn area, and then we watched the kid get off, and he sunk straight into the water." The incident has left parents questioning why schools opened on Monday despite the flooding. Concerns include why buses were sent into severely flooded streets and whether students should have sheltered in place at school until conditions improved. "Seeing the danger that all of the kids were put in is not okay," Lopez said. Abel added, "They really dropped the ball on this. The community is disappointed." On Tuesday, St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince addressed the situation during a news conference, apologizing to families for the district’s response. The first flood advisory for the county came in just after 8 a.m. Monday, with the first flash flood warning issued at 10:41 a.m. "I completely understand the frustration families feel," Prince said. "It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry." Despite the apology, some parents remain unsatisfied. "An apology doesn’t fix what is happening," Abel said. Lopez emphasized the need for change: "We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs." WPBF is working to hear from the school district to address these concerns and questions. Lucie is providing financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners for critical home repairs caused by this week’s flooding through its Disaster Relief Program, funded by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. The program, part of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP), offers support to low- and moderate-income homeowners for emergency repairs to their primary residences in Port St. Eligible expenses include tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability, payment of homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. These repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, temporary structural stabilization, and other actions necessary to protect the home from additional damage. Eligible homeowners may receive up to $25,000 through 0% interest deferred payment loans, with no monthly payments required. Loans are forgiven over a five-year period in accordance with program guidelines. All work must be directly related to the declared disaster, deemed necessary to preserve the safety and integrity of the property, and approved by the city before assistance is provided. Funding is not available for mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal, or remediation. Homeowners must complete any necessary mold remediation before approved repairs can proceed. Eligible repairs may be funded after remediation is complete. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or non-permitted work are not eligible for assistance. The city has allocated $1 million for the program, which will run until the funds are exhausted. The program’s pre-application will open at 8 a.m. To qualify, applicants must meet income guidelines, have owned and occupied their home within city limits for at least one year, have an assessed home value of $560,154 or less, and be current on mortgage and property tax payments. 5, residents may complete the pre-application online. Assistance is also available by contacting the city’s Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, emailing Housing@cityofpsl.com, or visiting City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Maria Andrade-Vasquez of Port St. Lucie has overcome plenty of challenges in her life. The mother of four, grandmother of 10, cancer survivor and dialysis patient never imagined a routine ride home from treatment would turn into a fight for survival. On Monday, Andrade-Vasquez was riding home from dialysis when floodwaters swept the transport van she was in off the road near Lakehurst Drive and into a canal in Port St. Lucie's Swan Park community. Speaking with CBS12 News through her son, Raul Morales, who translated from Spanish, Andrade-Vasquez said she feared she would not survive. "Yes, very, very scared," she said. Morales said as floodwaters rose around the van, his mother thought she might be living her final moments. Also see: Officer, firefighters rescue two from vehicle swept into Port St. Lucie canal "Seeing all the water go up, she was thinking, what's going to happen? Is this it?" Morales said. Police body camera video released this week shows how quickly first responders reacted. Lucie police said Officer Peterson arrived just 100 seconds after being dispatched to reports of a transport van that had gone into a canal off Southwest Hogan Street. Video captured the officer rushing into the water and rescuing the driver first before learning another passenger was still trapped inside. That passenger was Andrade-Vasquez. As water surrounded the vehicle, rescuers say the van tilted into the canal, leaving her trapped in the back. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the same wheelchair equipment used to help Andrade-Vasquez after dialysis treatments was now blocking her escape. "She's wheelchair bound, so the equipment that came out of the back of the van was up in place blocking her in," Niemczyk said. "They had to get her out of the wheelchair and pull her up over the equipment to get her out of the van." According to police, firefighters with St. Lucie County Fire District joined the officer at the scene and worked together to free Andrade-Vasquez from the vehicle. Morales said his mother still struggles to understand how rescuers were able to get her out so quickly. "She said, 'I don't know how they did it, but they quickly released her,'" Morales said. "To me it was amazing to see how quick they did what they did." Both Andrade-Vasquez and the driver were rescued safely. Her rescue was one of dozens of flood-related emergencies first responders handled as rainfall inundated roads and neighborhoods across Port St. Now recovering at home with her family, Andrade-Vasquez remains grateful to the first responders who helped save her life. The way I see it, you guys went the extra mile," Morales said. So thank you." Morales said his mother is still processing the trauma of the rescue but plans to continue her dialysis treatments three times a week as she focuses on her recovery.
