Residents in a Fort Pierce neighborhood were awakened early Wednesday morning by loud explosions as law enforcement agencies carried out a large-scale operation involving five search warrants across St. Neighbors along Miami Court described the startling events. "When you heard the sound, it sounded like a bomb; I thought, 'That's not a regular handgun, that sounds like a bomb,'" one neighbor said. "There were so many of them they were like a military. There was a military truck out there too," the neighbor added. Law enforcement vehicles were seen investigating at two homes in the area — one at 1708 Miami Court and another nearby at 1904 Georgia Avenue. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed the operation was part of a large-scale criminal investigation, with the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives also present at the scene. That same neighbor shared her experience, saying, "I heard what sounded like bombs going off. Boom, and I said, 'What the heck is going on?' I peeked out the door, and I saw the blue lights from the police." She said the noises woke her up, and she watched as officers blocked off the road and issued commands over a loudspeaker. Authorities have not released details about the investigation or what led to the arrests, but the sheriff's office stated there is no known threat to the community.

Recent flooding has displaced residents and wildlife, with animals appearing in unfamiliar areas. In Indian River County, floodwaters also pushed an alligator out of its usual habitat and into a residential driveway. On Friday, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office was on the scene, safely removing the animal from the residence and relocated it to a more suitable area within the county. No one was hurt, and the alligator was unharmed. Body camera video shows Indian River County deputies approaching what appears to be a huge gator. As they capture the critter, video shows the gator thrashing and hissing before deputies get it into a caged van. The video continues to show deputies releasing the alligator back into the wild. hero.headline: Deputies remove flood-displaced alligator from Indian River County residential driveway
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff's Office deputies safely removed an alligator from a residential driveway Friday after floodwaters pushed it out of its usual habitat. No one was hurt, and the alligator was unharmed.

Body camera video shows deputies approaching the alligator, which thrashed and hissed as they captured it and placed it in a caged van. Deputies relocated the animal to a more suitable area within Indian River County. The video also shows them releasing it back into the wild.

Recent flooding has displaced residents and wildlife, bringing animals into unfamiliar areas. Alligators were confirmed in flooded residential streets in Port St. Lucie on Thursday. An otter was also spotted after the flooding, and Martin County officials shared video of it navigating the changed landscape.

On Friday, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office was on the scene, safely removing the animal from the residence and relocated it to a more suitable area within the county. hero.headline: St. Lucie County search-warrant operation includes two Fort Pierce homes
hero.body:
Law enforcement agencies carried out an operation involving five search warrants in St. Lucie County early Wednesday, with activity at two Fort Pierce homes. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed the operation was part of a large-scale criminal investigation involving the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

Law enforcement vehicles were seen at 1708 Miami Court and nearby at 1904 Georgia Avenue. Residents along Miami Court said loud explosions woke them during the operation. The sheriff's office said there was no known threat to the community.

“When you heard the sound, it sounded like a bomb; I thought, 'That's not a regular handgun, that sounds like a bomb,'” one neighbor said. She described a large law enforcement presence outside. “There were so many of them they were like a military. There was a military truck out there too,” she said.

The neighbor said she looked outside after the noises woke her and saw police lights. She watched as officers blocked off the road and issued commands over a loudspeaker.

hero.headline: Search warrants executed in St. Lucie County; residents urged to avoid active scenes

The operation involved personnel from both agencies, with the sheriff’s office advising residents that they could notice more law enforcement officers in some areas while the work continued. Authorities asked people to stay away from places where officers were actively working and to follow instructions from personnel at those scenes. The sheriff’s office also said the operation posed no threat to the community.

During the operation, Fort Pierce police officers arrested a woman and put her in a police car. The arrest took place as law enforcement agencies were carrying out the search warrants Wednesday morning. Fort Pierce police were working with the sheriff’s office on the broader operation, which involved multiple warrants connected to a criminal investigation. Along with the arrest, the activity prompted a notice to residents about the police presence they might encounter. That notice asked the public to give officers room to work by avoiding locations where law enforcement activity was taking place.

The sheriff’s office advised residents that an increased law enforcement presence could remain visible in some areas as the operation continued. Its guidance was to avoid active scenes and comply with directions given by personnel there. For people who encountered officers working in their area, the agency’s request was the same: stay away from the activity and follow instructions at the scene. The advisory concerned the ongoing search-warrant operation involving the sheriff’s office and Fort Pierce police. Authorities paired that request for the public’s cooperation with an assurance that there was no threat to the community.

The multiple search warrants, the woman’s arrest and the public advisory were all part of Wednesday morning’s law enforcement activity in St. Lucie County. The sheriff’s office described the searches as part of a criminal investigation and said its personnel were collaborating with Fort Pierce police. As that work continued, residents were urged to remain clear of active law enforcement locations rather than approach the scenes. The agency’s message distinguished the visible police activity from a community threat: residents might see additional officers in some areas, but the sheriff’s office said the public was not in danger from the operation.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County relocating flood shelters to help public schools reopen
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management was relocating its general population and special medical needs shelters Wednesday morning to help public schools reopen as significant standing water persisted in parts of Port St. Lucie. Officials warned that water levels could take several days to recede.

The general population shelter was moving from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter was being relocated from the Fenn Center. On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by the flooding.

Water levels had receded in some areas, but significant standing water remained at SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Public works and water management agencies had opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides were limiting where the water could drain.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continued checking on residents, monitoring roadways and assisting people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations were also supporting recovery efforts and working to restore normal conditions safely.

Officials urged residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encouraged residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who might need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by the flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Floodwater rises in Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach; watershed limits pumping
hero.body:
Floodwater was still rising inside some Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon, long after the rain stopped. Martin County said it could not yet pump water out of the flooded neighborhood because the nearby watershed lacked capacity to receive it.

Dozens of homes in the neighborhood flooded after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the local drainage system. Residents Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid have been using a kayak to get around their flooded community. At Kincaid's home, the water was waist-deep. “We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,” Kincaid said.

Water inside French's home had reached 4 inches deep and was continuing to climb. Her husband made a mark inside to track the rising level. “My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,” French said.

Martin County said the neighborhood sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where water from other flooded areas is naturally flowing south. The county's ability to pump water out of the community depends on water levels dropping in the ponds that would receive it, according to Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon.

“As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

hero.headline: Student swims from school bus in Port St. Lucie floodwater, raising safety questions
hero.body:
A student entered deep floodwater after leaving a school bus in Port St. Lucie on Monday, prompting parents to question St. Lucie Public Schools’ decisions to open schools during severe weather and send buses into flooded streets. A viral video shows the student swimming home through the neighborhood, where the water has since receded.

Neighbor Ariel Abel said the bus became stuck before the student stepped into the water. “We watched the school bus get stuck over in that turn area, and then we watched the kid get off, and he sunk straight into the water.” Lucinda Lopez also described the danger: “He literally almost went completely underwater,” she said.

Parents have questioned whether students should have sheltered at school until conditions improved rather than boarding buses traveling through severely flooded streets. The county’s first flood advisory came just after 8 a.m. Monday, and the first flash flood warning was issued at 10:41 a.m. “Seeing the danger that all of the kids were put in is not okay,” Lopez said.

St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince apologized to families for the district’s response during a news conference Tuesday. “I completely understand the frustration families feel,” Prince said. “It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry.”

Some parents remained dissatisfied with the apology and called for changes to protect students. “An apology doesn’t fix what is happening,” Abel said. Lopez emphasized safety over attendance: “We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs.”
hero.article_text: A viral video showing a student swimming home from a school bus in flooded Port St. Lucie streets has raised questions about why schools opened during Monday’s severe weather. The video, filmed in a neighborhood where water has since receded, shows the student navigating deep floodwaters after exiting the bus. "He literally almost went completely underwater," said Lucinda Lopez, a Port St. Another neighbor, Ariel Abel, described the scene: "We watched the school bus get stuck over in that turn area, and then we watched the kid get off, and he sunk straight into the water." The incident has left parents questioning why schools opened on Monday despite the flooding. Concerns include why buses were sent into severely flooded streets and whether students should have sheltered in place at school until conditions improved. "Seeing the danger that all of the kids were put in is not okay," Lopez said. Abel added, "They really dropped the ball on this. The community is disappointed." On Tuesday, St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince addressed the situation during a news conference, apologizing to families for the district’s response. The first flood advisory for the county came in just after 8 a.m. Monday, with the first flash flood warning issued at 10:41 a.m. "I completely understand the frustration families feel," Prince said. "It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry." Despite the apology, some parents remain unsatisfied. "An apology doesn’t fix what is happening," Abel said. Lopez emphasized the need for change: "We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs." WPBF is working to hear from the school district to address these concerns and questions. cards.headline: Fort Pierce gang investigation leads to 11 racketeering arrests; two still wanted
cards.teaser: Authorities detailed charges in Operation Score Board and said people associated with the 23rd Street gang were linked to nearly 100 shootings over a decade.
cards.body:
The investigation into Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street gang that led to nearly 40 arrests included 11 arrests on racketeering charges, authorities said Thursday, with two people still wanted on warrants. The nearly two-year investigation, called Operation Score Board, focused on alleged gang activity in northwest Fort Pierce and surrounding areas. Officials said investigators linked 13 people to an alleged criminal conspiracy involving fraud, drug trafficking, shootings and homicides.

Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said investigators reviewed 10 years of criminal activity and connected people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings. Investigators also found that gang members allegedly kept a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, which inspired the operation’s name. Officials said about 70 to 80 people are documented as gang members. The investigation focused on people police described as shot callers who allegedly directed the gang’s activities. Authorities described the 23rd Street gang as the most violent of several gangs in Fort Pierce and said it had been a problem in the area for decades.

Officers served five search warrants, four in Fort Pierce and one in Port St. Lucie, beginning around 5 a.m. Along with the racketeering arrests, officials said the operation resulted in four additional probable-cause arrests. Some people connected to the investigation had already been arrested during its earlier stages. The searches yielded seven firearms, about one pound of marijuana, 15 grams of cocaine, 50 grams of MDMA and $18,474. Across the investigation, police said they seized 18 firearms, 20 pounds of marijuana, 532 grams of cocaine and two grams of MDPV.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the case required extensive work connecting years of records and evidence, including a 2,000-page report and a 150-page affidavit. Local, state and federal agencies participated, including ATF, FBI, DEA, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations. Officials also credited the State Attorney’s Office with helping build the case. Authorities said they believe most of the key players have been arrested, and Del Toro said more operations are expected. “We remain committed to identifying, investigating, and holding accountable those responsible for bringing violence and criminal activity into our neighborhoods,” Smith said.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie dialysis patient recalls canal rescue as body-camera video is released
cards.teaser: Maria Andrade-Vasquez feared she would not survive when floodwaters swept her transport van into a canal. Body-camera video released this week shows the response that brought her and the driver to safety.
cards.body:
Maria Andrade-Vasquez feared she would not survive when floodwaters swept her dialysis transport van into a Port St. Lucie canal Monday. Now recovering at home, she is recounting the rescue as police body-camera video released this week shows how an officer and firefighters helped save her. “Yes, very, very scared,” Andrade-Vasquez said, speaking through her son, Raul Morales, who translated from Spanish.

Andrade-Vasquez was riding home from treatment when the van was swept off the road near Lakehurst Drive in the Swan Park community. Police said Officer Peterson arrived just 100 seconds after being dispatched to reports of a transport van in a canal off Southwest Hogan Street. The video shows Peterson rushing into the water and rescuing the driver before learning that Andrade-Vasquez was still trapped inside. As water surrounded the vehicle, rescuers said, the van tilted into the canal, leaving her trapped in the back.

Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said wheelchair equipment in the van blocked Andrade-Vasquez’s escape. “She's wheelchair bound, so the equipment that came out of the back of the van was up in place blocking her in,” Niemczyk said. “They had to get her out of the wheelchair and pull her up over the equipment to get her out of the van.” Firefighters with St. Lucie County Fire District joined Peterson and worked with him to free her, according to police. Both Andrade-Vasquez and the driver were rescued safely.

Morales said his mother still struggles to understand how rescuers freed her so quickly. “To me it was amazing to see how quick they did what they did,” he said. Andrade-Vasquez, a mother of four, grandmother of 10 and cancer survivor, remains grateful to the first responders who saved her. Morales said she is still processing the trauma of the rescue and plans to continue dialysis treatments three times a week as she recovers at home with her family.

hero.body:
All northbound lanes of I-95 are closed at mile marker 105 in Martin County after a three-vehicle crash injured seven people, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. The crash site is roughly three miles north of High Meadow Avenue.

The seven people have non-life-threatening injuries and are being transported to nearby hospitals, the sheriff’s office said.

FHP will investigate the crash. The sheriff’s office said all northbound lanes are expected to stay closed for some time.

cards.headline: Floodwater rises in Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach as county waits to pump
cards.teaser: Water reached waist-deep at one home and continued climbing at another Wednesday. Martin County said the receiving watershed must have capacity before crews can pump water out.
cards.body:
Floodwater was still rising inside some Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon after Monday's heavy rain overwhelmed the drainage system. Martin County said it could not pump water out of the neighborhood because the nearby watershed lacked capacity.

Dozens of homes in the neighborhood were flooded after the rain saturated the ground and inundated local drainage. The community sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where water from other flooded areas is naturally flowing south, according to the county.

Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said pumping depends on water levels dropping in the ponds that would receive water from the neighborhood.

“As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

Residents Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid were using a kayak to get around their flooded community. At Kincaid's home, the water was waist-deep as she worked to save belongings.

“We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,” Kincaid said.

At French's home, water had reached 4 inches deep and continued to climb. Her husband marked the water level inside to track its rise.

“My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,” French said.

cards.headline: Flooding closes South 25th Street near two St. Lucie County schools
cards.teaser: The closure runs between Fort Pierce Central High School and Forest Grove Middle School. St. Lucie Public Schools extended school closures through Thursday, Nov. 5.
cards.body:
Flooding has closed South 25th Street to through traffic between Fort Pierce Central High School at Cobra Pride Way and the entrance to Forest Grove Middle School at Bulldog Drive in St. Lucie County.

County officials announced the closure Wednesday, citing unsafe road conditions caused by flooding. St. Lucie Public Schools also extended school closures through Thursday, Nov. 5, as the county continued dealing with widespread flooding.

Drivers are urged to use caution in the area and find alternate routes. Anyone with questions about the road closure can contact the county's Public Works Engineering Division at 772-462-1707.

hero.headline: Martin County delays drainage repairs as Trailside flooding threatens cattle, access
hero.body:
Martin County will wait until water levels recede to repair a drainage breach as flooding in the Trailside community threatens cattle and access to farm property. The county and the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District jointly determined that repairs should wait because hauling and placing sand under current conditions would be unsafe and could damage the levee.

The county said repair material could wash into the irrigation canal before crews establish a stable repair. Staff will continue monitoring water levels and site conditions with the conservancy district, and repairs will proceed when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. The county recently acquired approximately 315 acres in the area, known as the Elise J. A county spokesperson said establishing access has been the immediate priority so staff can assess conditions and respond. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flooding risks.

At Hungryland Farms, much of the pasture used for a 20-acre rotational grazing system for Florida Cracker cattle is underwater, according to owner Melissa. The flooding has forced the cattle onto the elevated driveway, and the farm is concerned about losing access. Some cattle have struggled to navigate the water. “We're starting to lose big sections of the driveway. We have them concentrated up the house pad, but if we lose too much more, we're just going to have to figure out a way to evacuate them somewhere,” she said.

The farm is bringing in hay and hay cubes to maintain the cattle’s regular diet while monitoring potential health risks from floodwaters. Melissa said the farm has an emergency contact with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service if the animals face imminent danger.

Kyla Shay, president of the Trailside Homeowners Association, said the community’s drainage system serves 41 lots and designated neighboring properties. She said water from outside that system is flowing through county-owned land and other neighboring properties into the community’s southern canal. Flooding has reached areas near Bridge Road and an electrical substation, she said.

Shay said some electrical transformers are partially underwater and submerged septic systems have left homeowners unable to shower or do laundry. She also said the health department warned her that standing water could compromise residents’ wells with bacteria. The association has been working with water engineers and other experts to understand how long the flooding could last, she said.

Authorities in St. Lucie County announced Thursday that 40 suspected members of Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street Gang have been arrested following an 18-month investigation. Investigators used Florida’s RICO law to connect years of alleged shootings, drug trafficking and other criminal activity to members of the gang.

The investigation, called “Operation Score Board,” involved multiple local and state law enforcement agencies. Investigators said the gang maintained a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, a discovery that gave the operation its name. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the gang has between 70 and 80 members and has been responsible for years of violence in Fort Pierce.

On Wednesday, officers executed multiple search warrants throughout the Fort Pierce area, making 11 arrests as part of the larger operation. Authorities said officers also seized multiple firearms, drugs and thousands of dollars in cash.

cards.headline: Flooding persists in Port St. Lucie as county moves shelters to help schools reopen
cards.teaser: Standing water remains on several Port St. Lucie roads, and officials warn drainage could take days. The general population shelter is moving to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
Flooding continues in parts of Port St. Lucie as St. Lucie County Emergency Management moves temporary shelters to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains along several roads and at other locations across the city. Officials warn it could take several days for water levels to recede.

Locations with significant standing water include SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain. Officials urge drivers to watch for flooded roads, obey barricades and stay off closed roadways.

The county’s Wednesday morning shelter relocation calls for moving the general population shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter is also relocating from the Fenn Center. On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue checking on residents, monitoring roadways and helping people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts. Officials encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

Vero Beach police released surveillance images and are asking for help identifying four people accused of damaging a room’s door and door frame at the Islander Inn, 3101 Ocean Drive. The Vero Beach Police Department classified the incident as criminal mischief.

The incident happened around 12:59 a.m., according to police. Investigators said surveillance footage captured four people at the property. Witnesses reported hearing loud banging or kicking noises before discovering damage to a room’s door and door frame.

Anyone who recognizes the people in the surveillance images or has information about the incident is asked to contact Detective Fonseca with the Vero Beach Police Department at 772-978-4667 or gfonseca@vbpd.org.

People wishing to remain anonymous can contact Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477. Tipsters may be eligible for a cash reward. The investigation remains ongoing.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests, including 11 for racketeering
hero.body:
A nearly two-year investigation into alleged 23rd Street gang activity in northwest Fort Pierce and surrounding areas has led to nearly 40 arrests, law enforcement officials announced Thursday. The investigation, called Operation Score Board, included 11 arrests on racketeering charges and targeted people authorities described as organizers who allegedly directed the gang’s activities. Two people remained wanted on warrants.

Officials said investigators linked 13 people to an alleged criminal conspiracy involving fraud, drug trafficking, shootings and homicides. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said investigators reviewed 10 years of criminal activity and connected people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings. Investigators also alleged that gang members kept a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, which inspired the operation’s name. Authorities said about 70 to 80 people are documented as members of the gang, which they described as the most violent of several gangs in Fort Pierce.

Officers served five search warrants, four in Fort Pierce and one in Port St. Lucie, beginning around 5 a.m. Officials said the operation resulted in the 11 racketeering arrests and four additional probable-cause arrests. Some people connected to the investigation had already been arrested during its earlier stages, authorities said. The searches yielded seven firearms, about one pound of marijuana, 15 grams of cocaine, 50 grams of MDMA and $18,474.

Across the investigation, police said they seized 18 firearms, 20 pounds of marijuana, 532 grams of cocaine and two grams of MDPV. Authorities said they believe they have arrested most of the key players.

Local, state and federal agencies participated, including ATF, FBI, DEA, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the case required extensive work connecting years of records and evidence, producing a 2,000-page report and a 150-page affidavit. Officials also credited the State Attorney’s Office with helping build the case.

“We remain committed to identifying, investigating, and holding accountable those responsible for bringing violence and criminal activity into our neighborhoods,” Smith said. “Our message is clear: We will not tolerate organized criminal activity that threatens the safety of our residents.”

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman recounts rescue from sinking van swept into canal by floodwaters
cards.teaser: Maria Andrade said she could not unlatch her seat belt as water filled the van. Body-camera footage shows an officer arriving less than two minutes after the 911 call and immediately entering the water.
cards.body:
Maria Andrade said she was trapped by a seat belt she could not unlatch as floodwaters filled a van that had been swept into a Port St. Lucie canal Monday morning. A police officer rescued the driver first, then helped firefighters pull Andrade from the van. Recounting the rescue through her son, Raul Morales, Andrade said the officer arrived so quickly that she did not have time to be scared.

Andrade was riding in the back of the van on her way home from a doctor's appointment when floodwaters pushed it into the canal. The driver called 911 for help. The officer's body-camera footage shows him arriving less than two minutes after the call and immediately entering the water. After the officer pulled the driver out, the driver told police the only way to get Andrade out was through the back. One person entered the van and pushed while others pulled her out.

Andrade, who speaks only Spanish, described heavy rain and floodwaters that made it difficult to distinguish the road. “She says it was raining really, really hard,” Morales said. “She couldn't even see the road. It was just water.” Andrade said she could hear water rushing into the van as it began to sink, and she was unable to release her seat belt.

Through Morales, Andrade thanked the first responders and said their quick arrival reassured her while she was trapped. “She wants to thank the first responders for being really, really on top of it. She realized how quick they were about it and made her feel better about her situation,” Morales said.
cards.article_text: Lucie police officer rescued two people trapped in a sinking van after floodwaters pushed their van into a canal Monday morning. In an exclusive interview, the woman who was rescued, Maria Andrade, told WPBF 25 News she was in the back of the van on her way home from a doctor's appointment when floodwaters pushed the van into a canal. The driver was able to call 911 and ask for help. The police officer's body camera footage shows him arriving less than two minutes after the call and immediately entering the water. The officer first pulled the driver out of the van and, with the help of firefighters, rescued Andrade, who was trapped inside. Andrade, who only speaks Spanish, explained through her son, Raul Morales, that the floodwaters had gotten so bad, it was hard to tell where the road was. “She says it was raining really, really hard,” Morales said. "She couldn't even see the road. It was just water." Andrade said the van began sinking and filling up with water. “She could hear the water just gushing in there. That’s what pretty much told me, 'Uh oh. I’m in trouble,'” Morales said. Maria said she couldn’t unlatch her seat belt and was trapped inside the van. But she also said she didn’t have time to be scared because the officer arrived so quickly. The van’s driver told police the only way to get Maria out was through the back. One person entered the van and pushed while others pulled her out. “She wants to thank the first responders for being really, really on top of it. She realized how quick they were about it and made her feel better about her situation,” Morales said. “Thank you for helping her out and for being there for her. there’s no words for it." hero.headline: Flooding forces Palm City's Happy Place Ranch to close as animal-care costs rise
hero.teaser: Happy Place Ranch has been losing revenue since October as weather canceled its fall festival and horse shows. Flooding has now closed the Palm City ranch and increased expenses for its animals.
hero.body:
Flooding has forced Happy Place Ranch in Palm City to close to visitors, cutting off income and increasing animal-care costs after months of weather-related disruptions. Days after heavy rain swept through the area, much of the property remains surrounded by standing water. Owner Amanda Cimorelli said the ranch has been losing revenue since October, with weather forcing cancellations of its fall festival and horse shows. The latest flooding has left the business facing more potential cancellations while it spends extra money caring for its animals. “It's crushing,” Cimorelli said, fighting back tears. “It's sad.”

The ranch has offered horse shows, riding lessons, birthday parties and other activities for seven years. Now, two upcoming birthday parties may have to be canceled because of the flooding. Cimorelli said that would be a first during the ranch's seven years at the property. The possible cancellations come as the business faces both lost bookings and additional expenses. “It's just thousands and thousands of dollars of revenue lost and extra cash going out that we really don't have right now,” she said. Hay is one of the added costs as the ranch works to provide what its animals need while the property is flooded.

All of the animals are OK, Cimorelli said, but finding dry areas for them has been difficult. The ranch has brought them into the barn as much as possible while water covers the grounds. “I have nowhere to put farm animals. We got everyone in the barn as much as we can,” she said. Cimorelli said they anticipated rain, but the amount exceeded their expectations. “We figured it was just rain. It was relentless,” she said. For now, work is centered on cleanup while they wait for the floodwater to drain away. “All we can do is wait,” she said. “Just wait and figure it out day by day.”

Flooding has also disrupted Gardino Nursery in Loxahatchee Groves, where owner Sid Gardino said a freeze and drought had already made the year difficult. Water rose to shin height in parts of the nursery, and thick mud has made walking around difficult. “We are working at 20% capacity,” Gardino said. The appointment-only business can still ship products, but customers cannot currently visit to view plants. Its revenue losses from the flooding have not yet been determined. Gardino said conditions on the property are starting to improve, and the nursery hopes to reopen by next week if sunny, warm weather continues.

cards.headline: Water kept rising in Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach after rain stopped
cards.body:
Water was still rising inside some homes on Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon, long after the rain stopped. Martin County said it could not pump water out of the flooded neighborhood because the nearby watershed lacked capacity to receive it.

Dozens of homes were flooded after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the drainage system. The neighborhood sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where water from other flooded areas is naturally flowing south, according to the county. Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said pumping depends on water levels falling in the ponds that would receive the water.

“As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

hero.headline: St. Lucie County moving flood shelters to help public schools reopen
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management was moving shelters for flood-displaced residents Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen, as flooding persisted in parts of the county. Officials warned that water levels could take several days to recede, with recent heavy rainfall and King Tides limiting where the water could drain.

The general population shelter was being moved from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter was also being relocated from the Fenn Center. On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels had receded in some areas, but significant standing water remained at several locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Public works and water management agencies had opened water control structures to help drainage. Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continued checking on residents, monitoring roadways and assisting people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations were also supporting recovery efforts.

Officials urged residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encouraged people to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by the flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Water rises in Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach as full watershed prevents pumping
hero.body:
Water was still rising inside some homes on Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon, long after the rain stopped. Martin County said it could not pump water out of the flooded neighborhood because the nearby watershed was at capacity.

Dozens of homes in the neighborhood were underwater after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the drainage system. Residents Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid were using a kayak to get around their flooded community.

At Kincaid's home, the water was waist-deep as she worked to save belongings. “We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,” Kincaid said.

Water inside French's home had reached 4 inches and was continuing to climb. “My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,” French said.

The neighborhood sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where water is naturally flowing south from other flooded areas, according to Martin County. The county said the nearby watershed lacked the capacity to receive water pumped from the community.

Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said falling water levels would allow the county to begin pumping into ponds.

“As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

Residents were confronting damage to their homes while the flooding continued. “It's just a lot to take in right now for us,” Kincaid said.

hero.headline: Indian River County schools to remain closed Friday as transportation problems persist
hero.body:
Indian River County schools will be closed Friday, Nov. 6, as transportation difficulties continue after flooding, the School District of Indian River County announced Thursday. The district expects classes to resume Monday, Nov. 9. Only a limited number of bus drivers are available, and traffic on County Roads 510 and 512 continues to face substantial delays. Flooding has left some roads, bus stops and school campuses difficult or unsafe to reach across Indian River and St. Lucie counties. Indian River County school buildings will be open to instructional staff so they can prepare for the anticipated return of students Monday.

St. Lucie Public Schools also will stay closed Friday and plans to reopen Monday, Nov. 9. Although conditions have improved in some areas, district officials said many roads and bus stops are still inaccessible because of floodwater. Access to some school campuses remains affected as well. Some families and district employees still have no electricity, while others cannot safely get out of their neighborhoods. Officials said conditions differ widely across the county: Some neighborhoods have returned to normal, but flooding elsewhere continues to make trips to school unsafe, whether students and employees walk, ride a bus or travel by car.

The two districts announced different schedules for activities. Indian River County said its activities and extracurricular programs would resume Thursday, while St. Lucie Public Schools canceled all athletic activities through Sunday. St. Lucie athletics can restart Monday. The SAT that had been scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, has been moved to Saturday, Nov. 21. St. Lucie school officials also said they would share further information if instructional make-up days become necessary. The district acknowledged that the extended closures are difficult for families and employees and thanked them for their patience and flexibility as flooding continues to affect travel and school access.

Five Boys & Girls Clubs locations will open beginning at 8 a.m. for current members and families interested in joining. Each site can accommodate 100 children, and members may go to any participating club rather than only the location they usually attend. Participating clubs include Chuck Hill; Ken Pruitt, at 10673 SE Lennard Road in Port St. Lucie; Percy Peek Teen, at 2902 Avenue D in Fort Pierce; and Garden Terrace, at 3104 Avenue J in Fort Pierce. Parents and guardians should send children with a packed lunch, a snack and a water bottle.

cards.headline: Vero Beach police seek IDs of four people in Islander Inn door-damage investigation
cards.teaser: Police released surveillance images after a room door and door frame were damaged at the hotel on Ocean Drive. Investigators are asking anyone who recognizes the four people to contact Detective Fonseca.
cards.body:
Vero Beach police have released surveillance images and are asking for help identifying four people in an investigation into damage to a room door and door frame at the Islander Inn, 3101 Ocean Drive.

The incident happened around 12:59 a.m., according to the Vero Beach Police Department. Investigators said surveillance footage captured four people at the property. Witnesses reported hearing loud banging or kicking noises before discovering the damage. The department classified the incident as criminal mischief, and the investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone who recognizes the people in the images or has information about the incident is asked to contact Detective Fonseca with the Vero Beach Police Department at 772-978-4667 or gfonseca@vbpd.org.

People wishing to remain anonymous can contact Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477. Tipsters may be eligible for a cash reward.

hero.headline: About 75% of Creekside homes evacuated as flooding keeps power off in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Roughly 75% of homes in the flooded Creekside community in St. Lucie County have been evacuated, and electricity remains shut off, Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Thursday. Utility equipment remains underwater, and crews must wait for water to recede enough to safely restore power.

The neighborhood, off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. Floodwaters are still knee-deep in parts of the community. Del Toro said some trucks can now enter the neighborhood, though water levels remain high.

FPL's Marshall Critchfield said crews are monitoring water levels and will restore electricity as soon as they can safely reach the equipment. “Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety,” Critchfield said. Del Toro said Creekside has underground utilities, adding to the challenge while floodwaters remain high.

Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, Del Toro said. The sheriff's office also has a high-water vehicle available to help residents who need assistance.

“If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies,” Del Toro said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Public Schools to remain closed Friday as flooding blocks access
cards.teaser: The district expects schools to reopen Monday, Nov. 9. Five Boys & Girls Clubs locations will open at 8 a.m. Friday, with space for 100 children at each site.
cards.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools will remain closed Friday, Nov. 6, because flooding continues to make roads, bus stops and access to some campuses unsafe or inaccessible. The district expects schools to reopen Monday, Nov. 9.

Although conditions have improved in parts of St. Lucie County, district officials said a significant number of roads and bus stops remain inaccessible. Some families and employees cannot safely leave their neighborhoods. “Conditions vary greatly across our county,” the St. Lucie Public Schools District said in its announcement. “Although some neighborhoods have returned to normal, others continue to experience flooding that makes traveling to school, whether on foot, by bus, or by car, unsafe.”

Five Boys & Girls Clubs locations will open at 8 a.m. Friday for current members and families interested in joining. Each location has capacity for 100 children. Members may attend any participating club, regardless of which location they normally attend. Participating locations include:

• Ken Pruitt: 10673 SE Lennard Road, Port St. Lucie
• Percy Peek Teen: 2902 Avenue D, Fort Pierce
• Garden Terrace: 3104 Avenue J, Fort Pierce

Parents and guardians are asked to send children with a packed lunch, a snack and a water bottle.

All St. Lucie Public Schools athletic activities are canceled through Sunday and can resume Monday. The SAT scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, has been postponed to Saturday, Nov. 21. The district said it will provide additional information if instructional make-up days are needed.

Schools in Indian River County also will remain closed Friday, with reopening expected Monday, Nov. 9. The School District of Indian River County said Thursday that transportation remains a concern, with a limited number of bus drivers available and significant delays continuing on County Roads 510 and 512. School buildings will be accessible to instructional staff as they prepare for Monday. The district said activities and extracurriculars will resume Thursday.

cards.headline: High-capacity pump starts in Port St. Lucie’s Vitalia as flooding forces evacuations
cards.teaser: The pump began operating Wednesday night to help reduce flooding in Vitalia. Routine evacuations were paused overnight and scheduled to resume Thursday morning.
cards.body:
A high-capacity pump began operating Wednesday night, Nov. 4, in Port St. Lucie’s flooded Vitalia community, where residents required evacuation because flooded roads prevented them from driving out. The City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department installed the 12-inch pump, which started running at approximately 8 p.m., according to the St. Lucie County Fire District.

The pump was moving an estimated 7,000 to 8,000 gallons of water per minute to help reduce neighborhood flooding, the fire district said. Routine evacuation operations in Vitalia were suspended overnight Wednesday and scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Thursday, Nov. 5. The district said emergency responders remained available for fire and medical emergencies. It directed residents with immediate safety concerns or serious medical needs requiring assistance to call 911.

Vitalia residents Sheri George and her husband, Arthur, were evacuated Wednesday by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission aboard a swamp buggy. Their home had lost electricity and air conditioning, food in their refrigerator was spoiling, and flooded roads kept them from leaving by car. Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident, also was evacuated because of flooding. FWC said it had evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater since Tuesday. As of Wednesday evening, the St. Lucie County Fire District had responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents countywide.

Flooding had continued for more than 48 hours. In Valencia Cay at Riverland, residents were unable to get cars out of their driveways because of flooded streets, and some said water reached their garages. Police warned that floodwater could take days to recede even after the heaviest rain had moved through. They also warned that conditions could change quickly. They urged residents to follow evacuation instructions, never drive or walk through floodwaters, avoid closed or barricaded roads, and check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones when they could do so safely.
cards.article_text: Lucie police are evacuating residents from the flooded Vitalia community as dangerous waters continue to affect neighborhoods more than 48 hours into the flooding emergency. I think it's part of living in Florida," said Sheri George, a Vitalia resident. Sheri George and her husband Arthur were evacuated by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission on a swamp buggy Wednesday. They had no electricity, no A/C and the food in their refrigerator was spoiling. They were unable to drive out of the neighborhood because roads were flooded. They were thrilled FWC could get them safely out of the neighborhood. This is definitely, whoever's idea this was, thank you. 'Cause otherwise we would've been stuck there, who knows how much longer," Sheri George said. "I don't understand why it happened. hero.headline: Water kept rising Wednesday in Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach
hero.body:
Water was still rising inside some homes on Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon after Monday's heavy rain flooded dozens of homes. Martin County said it could not pump water out of the neighborhood because the nearby watershed lacked capacity to receive it.

The rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the local drainage system, leaving much of the neighborhood underwater. The community sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where the county said water from other flooded areas was naturally flowing south.

Residents Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid were using a kayak to get around the flooded community. At Kincaid's home, the water was waist-deep. “We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,” Kincaid said.

At French's home, water had reached 4 inches deep and continued to climb. Her husband marked the water level inside to track its rise. “My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,” French said.

Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said pumping would depend on water levels falling in the ponds that would receive water from the neighborhood. “As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

Residents were salvaging belongings as flooding continued two days after the rain. “It's just a lot to take in right now for us,” Kincaid said.

hero.headline: Indian River County public schools to remain closed Friday, plan Monday reopening
hero.body:
Indian River County public schools will stay closed Friday, Nov. 6, because flooding is still interfering with transportation and access to some campuses. The district plans to welcome students back Monday, Nov. 9. Officials cited a shortage of available bus drivers and major delays on County Roads 510 and 512 as reasons for keeping schools closed Friday. School buildings will be open to instructional staff so they can prepare for the planned return Monday. The reopening remains a plan as the district continues to watch conditions and provide updates through its official communication channels.

St. Lucie County public schools also will remain closed Friday, with classes expected to resume Monday. Flooding has made some roads and bus stops inaccessible and has complicated access to some school campuses. The problems extend beyond school property: Some families and district employees still have no electricity, while others cannot safely get out of their neighborhoods. Those ongoing transportation and access issues are affecting the district’s return to school. St. Lucie officials said they will continue monitoring conditions and issuing updates through official channels. The district also will provide information about any required instructional make-up days when that information becomes available.

The St. Lucie district canceled athletic activities through Sunday, with athletics potentially returning Monday. The SAT that had been scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, has been rescheduled. The planned Monday return for both school districts follows continued flooding that has disrupted travel to schools and left some families unable to leave home safely. In Indian River County, the district’s Friday arrangements allow instructional staff into buildings to prepare even though schools remain closed to students. In St. Lucie County, the district’s announcement also addresses the disruption to athletics and the weekend SAT, in addition to Friday’s school closure.

Five Boys & Girls Clubs locations in St. Lucie County will open at 8 a.m. for current members and children interested in joining. Each site can serve up to 100 members, and members may attend any location. Families can register at bgcofslc.org. Children should bring their own packed lunch, a snack and a water bottle. Locations include Chuck Hill at 198 Marion Ave.; Ken Pruitt at 10673 SE Lennard Road in Port St. Lucie; Percy Peek Teen at 2902 Avenue D in Fort Pierce; and Garden Terrace at 3104 Avenue J in Fort Pierce. The clubs’ announcement gives families a separate option while public schools remain closed.

hero.headline: About 75% of Creekside homes evacuated as flooding keeps power off in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Roughly 75% of homes in St. Lucie County’s Creekside community have been evacuated, and electricity remains shut off amid flooding, St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Thursday. Some Florida Power & Light equipment remains underwater, and crews must wait for water to recede enough to safely restore power.

The neighborhood, off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. Floodwaters are still knee-deep in parts of the community. Del Toro said some trucks can now enter the neighborhood, though water levels remain high.

Deputies are providing 24-hour security while residents remain displaced and electricity is out. A high-water vehicle is also available to help residents who need assistance. Del Toro urged residents to contact deputies or call 911 if they need help.

“We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else,” Florida Power & Light's Marshall Critchfield said. “Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety.”

Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as the water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said Creekside has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while floodwaters remain high.

cards.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools expects to reopen Friday, Nov. 6, after remaining closed Thursday because of flooding, but the district cautioned that road conditions could change that plan. Numerous flooded bus stops and areas of high water prompted the continued closure.

The district announced Wednesday that campuses would remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5, as St. Lucie County recovers from flooding caused by this week’s severe weather. District officials said they wanted to allow more time for floodwaters to subside before returning to normal operations.

Essential employees are required to report to work as outlined in the district’s Emergency Operations Plan. Families are encouraged to check the St. Lucie Public Schools website for updates before schools reopen.

“Thank you for your patience and understanding as our community recovers from this unprecedented weather event,” the district said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County plans flood shelter move to Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to help public schools reopen. The county is also relocating its special medical needs shelter.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management plans to move its general population flood shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The relocation was scheduled for Wednesday morning, along with a move for the special medical needs shelter currently at the Fenn Center.

On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts.

Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where water can drain. Officials urge residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads, stay out of closed roadways and never go around barricades. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: About 75% of Creekside homes evacuated in St. Lucie County; power remains off
hero.body:
Roughly 75% of homes in the flooded Creekside community in St. Lucie County have been evacuated, and power remains shut off, Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Thursday. Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the neighborhood, and submerged Florida Power & Light equipment must become safely accessible before crews can restore electricity.

The community has about 150 homes off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike and remains under a voluntary evacuation, Del Toro said. Some trucks can now enter the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. The neighborhood has underground utilities, which Del Toro said creates an additional challenge while flooding persists.

FPL's Marshall Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as the water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. “We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else,” Critchfield said. “Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety.”

Deputies are providing 24-hour security in Creekside while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, Del Toro said. The sheriff's office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. “If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies,” Del Toro said.

hero.headline: Vitalia evacuations paused overnight as Port St. Lucie starts floodwater pump
hero.body:
Routine evacuations in Port St. Lucie’s flooded Vitalia community were suspended overnight as a newly installed pump began moving water out of the neighborhood Wednesday evening, the St. Lucie County Fire District said. Evacuations were scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Thursday. Emergency responders remain available for fire and medical emergencies, and residents with immediate safety concerns or serious medical needs requiring assistance should call 911.

The City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department installed the 12-inch pump, which began operating at approximately 8 p.m. Wednesday to help reduce flooding in Vitalia, according to the fire district. Flooding had continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain had moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly. As of Wednesday evening, the fire district had responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents countywide. Police urged residents to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission evacuated Vitalia resident Sheri George and her husband Arthur on a swamp buggy Wednesday. Flooded roads had prevented them from driving out of the neighborhood, and food in their refrigerator was spoiling during a power outage. “This is definitely, whoever's idea this was, thank you. 'Cause otherwise we would've been stuck there, who knows how much longer,” Sheri George said. Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident evacuated because of flooding, questioned the community’s preparedness. “I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me,” Guogas said.

FWC said it had evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater since Tuesday. Jon Arnold, an FWC investigator, was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia. “I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety,” said Tyson Matthews, FWC Public Information Officer.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County plans flood shelter move to Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to help public schools reopen. The special medical needs shelter is also relocating from the Fenn Center.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management planned to move its general population flood shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce on Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The special medical needs shelter, housed at the Fenn Center, was also set to relocate.

On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several Port St. Lucie locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts.

Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where water can drain. Officials urge residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Water keeps rising in Jensen Beach homes on Hyline Drive after rain stops
hero.body:
Water was still rising inside some homes on Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon, long after the rain stopped, with dozens of homes flooded. Monday’s heavy rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the drainage system. Martin County said it was unable to pump water out of the neighborhood because the nearby watershed lacked capacity.

The neighborhood sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where water is naturally flowing south from other flooded areas, according to the county. Martin County’s Public Works Director Jim Gordon said lower water levels would allow the county to begin pumping. “As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

Residents Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid were using a kayak to get around their flooded community. Water at Kincaid’s home was waist-deep as she worked to save belongings. “We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,” Kincaid said.

At French’s home, water had reached 4 inches deep and was continuing to climb. Her husband made a mark inside to track the rising level. “My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,” French said.

Both residents were confronting damage to their homes while the flooding continued. “Even after, like, our houses are wrecked,” French said. Kincaid described the strain: “It's just a lot to take in right now for us.”

hero.headline: Vitalia routine evacuations paused overnight as pump starts in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
Routine evacuations in Port St. Lucie’s flooded Vitalia community were suspended overnight and were scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Thursday, according to the St. Lucie County Fire District. A newly installed pump began operating Wednesday evening as dangerous flooding continued to affect neighborhoods more than 48 hours into the emergency. Fire and medical emergency response remained available during the pause in routine evacuations. The fire district directed residents with immediate safety concerns or serious medical needs requiring assistance to call 911.

The City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department installed the 12-inch pump in Vitalia, where it began operating at approximately 8 p.m. Wednesday, the fire district said. The pump was moving an estimated 7,000 to 8,000 gallons of water per minute to help reduce neighborhood flooding. As of Wednesday evening, the fire district had responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents across St. Lucie County. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said it had evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater since Tuesday. Police warned that water could take days to recede and that conditions could change quickly, even after the heaviest rain had moved through.

Vitalia resident Sheri George and her husband Arthur were evacuated Wednesday aboard a Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission swamp buggy. Flooded roads had prevented them from driving out of the neighborhood, and food in their refrigerator was spoiling. Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident evacuated because of flooding, questioned the preparation for the emergency. “I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me,” Guogas said.

Flooding also affected Valencia Cay at Riverland, where some residents were unable to get their cars out of their driveways because streets were flooded. Some residents said water reached their garages. Street flooding reached 18 inches deep. Police urged residents to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads. They also encouraged residents to check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones when they could do so safely.

cards.headline: Water rises in Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach as full watershed blocks pumping
cards.teaser: Water was still rising inside some homes Wednesday afternoon after Monday's heavy rain overwhelmed drainage. Martin County said the nearby watershed was too full to receive water pumped from the neighborhood.
cards.body:
Water was still rising inside some homes on Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon, long after the rain stopped. Martin County said it could not pump water out of the flooded neighborhood because the nearby watershed lacked capacity to receive it.

Dozens of homes were underwater after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the drainage system. The neighborhood sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where water from other flooded areas is naturally flowing south, according to the county.

Residents Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid have been using a kayak to get around their flooded community. Water at Kincaid's home was waist-deep. “We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,” Kincaid said.

At French's home, water had reached 4 inches deep and was continuing to rise. French said her husband had marked the water level inside to track its climb. “My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,” she said.

Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said lower water levels would allow the county to pump into nearby ponds. “As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

cards.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls
cards.body:
St. Lucie County emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding, officials said Tuesday. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday, Nov. 4. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel, saying water could take several days to recede. Public Safety Director Ron Guerrero said estimated rainfall totals reached 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards, as well as Virginia Avenue.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. The county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Crews continued high-water rescues, assessed roads and infrastructure, and worked to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns.

Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised avoiding standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and washing with soap and water after exposure. Residents should not eat food or use household items that touched floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water, boil tap water or disinfect it. Flood-affected private wells should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

The school district hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions, and planned to assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Officials warned that road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. The city also warned of a one-day solid waste collection delay, with collection shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. Guerrero said the county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Officials were continuing high-water rescues, assessing roads and infrastructure, and working with public works crews to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns, he said. Please use caution and avoid unnecessary travel, Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the county landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. He said the district had not seen significant water intrusion in its schools but would assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Lucie officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. The city said vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000 . The city also warned residents to expect a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday. Officials urge residents to avoid floodwater Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and neighborhoods that had been evacuated. He warned against taking advantage of residents affected by flooding and said the Sheriff’s Office would take those cases seriously. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Sperber said health officials planned to assess mobile home parks for flood-related health and safety concerns. Residents with questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can call 772-873-4931 . Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.
