hero.headline: Evacuations continue in Port St. Lucie's Vitalia as floodwaters could linger for days
hero.body:
Police are evacuating residents from the flooded Vitalia community in Port St. Lucie as dangerous water persists more than 48 hours into the flooding emergency. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said it has evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater across several affected areas since Tuesday. Police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly.

FWC evacuated Vitalia resident Sheri George and her husband, Arthur, aboard a swamp buggy Wednesday. Flooded roads had prevented them from driving out of the neighborhood. They had no electricity or air conditioning, and food in their refrigerator was spoiling. George said she was thankful for the evacuation, which got the couple safely out of the community. Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident, also was evacuated because of flooding. “I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me,” Guogas said.

FWC investigator Jon Arnold was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia as crews helped residents leave. FWC Public Information Officer Tyson Matthews credited cooperation among communities, first responders and law enforcement. “I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety,” Matthews said.

In Valencia Cay at Riverland, some residents said flooded streets left them effectively trapped at home and unable to get their cars out of their driveways. Some said water had reached their garages but had not entered their homes. Although the heaviest rain has moved through, police said officers and emergency personnel continued helping residents get to safety. Police urged residents to follow evacuation instructions, never drive or walk through floodwaters, avoid closed or barricaded roads, and check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones when they can do so safely.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie offers up to $25,000 for flood repairs through $1 million program
cards.teaser: Eligible homeowners can receive forgivable loans for emergency repairs after this week’s flooding. Mold remediation is excluded and must be completed before approved repairs can proceed.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie has allocated $1 million to help income-eligible homeowners repair damage from this week’s flooding, offering up to $25,000 per eligible homeowner through its Disaster Relief Program. The assistance comes as 0% interest deferred-payment loans with no monthly payments, forgiven over five years under program guidelines.

The program serves low- and moderate-income homeowners making emergency repairs to their primary residences within city limits. Applicants must meet income guidelines, have owned and occupied their homes for at least one year, and have an assessed home value of $560,154 or less. They must also be current on mortgage and property tax payments. Funded by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation as part of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP), the program will continue until its funding is exhausted.

Mold and mildew inspection, testing, removal and remediation are excluded from funding. Homeowners must complete any necessary mold remediation before approved repairs can proceed, though eligible repairs may be funded once remediation is complete. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or non-permitted work are also ineligible for assistance.

Covered expenses include tree and debris removal needed to restore habitability, homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. Repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, and temporary structural stabilization. All work must be directly related to the declared disaster, necessary to preserve the property’s safety and integrity, and approved by the city before assistance is provided.

Residents may complete the program’s pre-application online. For assistance, homeowners can contact the city’s Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, email Housing@cityofpsl.com or visit City Hall.

cards.teaser: The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School as St. Lucie County relocates two shelters to help public schools reopen. Twenty-one people were staying at the shelters Wednesday.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population flood shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce on Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The county is also relocating its special medical needs shelter from the Fenn Center as residents displaced by this week’s flooding continue to need accommodation.

On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help displaced residents.

Flooding continues in parts of St. Lucie County. Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts.

Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Officials are urging residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by the flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Water rises in Jensen Beach homes on Hyline Drive as Martin County cannot pump it out
hero.body:
Water was still rising inside some homes on Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon, long after the rain stopped. Martin County said it cannot pump water out of the flooded neighborhood because the nearby watershed remains at capacity.

Dozens of homes are underwater after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the drainage system. The neighborhood sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where water from other flooded areas is naturally flowing south, according to the county.

Residents Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid have been using a kayak to get around their flooded community. At Kincaid's home, the water is waist-deep. “We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,” Kincaid said.

At French's home, water had reached 4 inches deep and was continuing to climb. French said her husband marked the water level inside to track its rise. Her floorboards were outside, and she said other homes were in worse condition.

Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said lower water levels would allow the ponds that receive pumped water to drain, creating room for the county to begin pumping out the neighborhood.

“As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

Residents are trying to salvage belongings while facing damage to their homes. “It's just a lot to take in right now for us,” Kincaid said.

cards.headline: Steven Giordano defeats Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race
cards.teaser: Giordano won by just over 2,400 votes, reversing an August primary result in which Martin finished nearly 13 percentage points ahead of him.
cards.body:
Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Shannon Martin for Port St. Lucie mayor by just over 2,400 votes, reversing their standings in the August primary. Martin had finished nearly 13 percentage points ahead of Giordano in that contest.

Giordano celebrated with supporters Tuesday night at Recovery Sports Grill in Tradition after pulling ahead with more than 51% of the vote. At his election-night watch party, he said he believed voters responded to his message and approach to the race. "I think they saw somebody that was dedicated, that was here for all the right reasons," Giordano said. "I think they watched the debate."

Giordano said he wants to serve residents rather than approach the position as a politician. "I think they saw somebody who is here for all the right reasons, that's not a politician, that's not here for money, that's here to do the right thing for the people," he said. "And I'm proud to be the people's mayor."

The general election followed a contentious August primary that included an FDLE investigation involving campaign signs. The investigation led to Martin's husband and two other Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on paid administrative leave.

cards.teaser: The general population shelter is relocating from Northport K-8 School to help public schools reopen. Sixteen people were staying at the shelter Wednesday.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population flood shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce on Wednesday to help St. Lucie Public Schools reopen. The relocation comes as flooding continues in parts of the county and recovery crews work to restore normal conditions.

Sixteen people were staying at the general population shelter Wednesday, while five were at the special medical needs shelter. The special medical needs shelter is also relocating from the Fenn Center. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations in Port St. Lucie, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts. Officials urge residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

cards.headline: Family questions walking safety on Port St. Lucie Boulevard after teen's death
cards.teaser: Jacory Brown's family is raising concerns about construction and walking conditions after the Treasure Coast High School freshman was killed Oct. 7. A road-widening project is expected to finish in winter 2028.
cards.body:
The family of Jacory Brown, a Treasure Coast High School freshman killed while walking to school Oct. 7, is raising concerns about walking conditions along Port St. Lucie Boulevard. His family says construction makes the road dangerous for children traveling to school on foot.

Brown was struck and killed by a car early that morning. His mother, Shelly-Ann Findley-Brown, described puddles and inadequate sidewalks along the road, saying rain the night before had left water in the area.

“The road conditions are horrible,” Findley-Brown said. “You are walking in puddles. And the night before, it rained. There was water all over the place.”

FDOT began construction in 2025 to widen the road from two lanes to four. The project, which includes adding sidewalks and lights, is expected to be completed in winter 2028.

“I hope the state takes this into a big consideration because it's not right walking to school when you don't have proper sidewalks,” Findley-Brown said.

Jacory's parents, Findley-Brown and Ainsworth Brown, and his grandfather, Clovis Brown, are remembering his smile and friendliness. Jacory also had a passion for entrepreneurship and graphic design, creating cover art, business cards and flyers for friends and family.

“He just went to school,” Findley-Brown said. “He was supposed to come back home. His birthday would be on Monday. He would have been 15.”

Jacory will be laid to rest Nov. 14. Friends have started a GoFundMe to support the family.

hero.headline: Martin County judge rejects dismissal of Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo’s cruelty case
hero.body:
A Martin County judge on Wednesday rejected a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, allowing the prosecution to continue after at least nine trial delays since her arrest more than two years ago.

Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense’s second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. hearing, prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed. Prosecutors had opposed the request to throw out the charges, arguing in a court filing that the defense’s amended motion was “procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.”

Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Necropsies determined that the two dogs died from blunt force trauma, leading to her arrest.

The case has faced repeated delays and disputes over expert witnesses. At a contentious hearing in July, Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo’s defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial.

“I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,” Metzger said. “This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count.”

In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial.

Camerlengo’s defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths.

Camerlengo’s next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. 1.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie to open applications Thursday for $1 million in flood-repair aid
cards.teaser: Eligible homeowners can receive up to $25,000 through loans forgiven over five years. Pre-applications open at 8 a.m. Thursday.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie will open pre-applications at 8 a.m. Thursday for its $1 million Disaster Relief Program, which helps low- and moderate-income homeowners repair primary residences damaged by this week's flooding. The city announced the allocation Wednesday. Eligible homeowners can receive up to $25,000, and the program will remain open until the funding is exhausted.

The assistance comes through the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, with funding from the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. It is offered as a 0% interest deferred-payment loan with no monthly payments. The loans are forgiven over five years in accordance with program guidelines. Applicants must meet the program's income requirements and must have owned and occupied their home within Port St. Lucie city limits for at least one year. The home's assessed value must be $560,154 or less, and applicants must be current on mortgage and property tax payments.

According to the city, the money can pay for emergency repairs and other work needed to make a flood-damaged home safe and habitable. Eligible expenses may include tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability, homeowners insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further damage. Those repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, and temporary structural stabilization. cards.headline: St. Lucie County flood shelter moving to Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School as flood recovery continues. Standing water remains at several Port St. Lucie locations, and officials warn drivers to stay off closed roads.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce on Wednesday as flood recovery continues. The move is part of a relocation of the county’s general population and special medical needs shelters to help St. Lucie public schools reopen.

On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The special medical needs shelter is relocating from the Fenn Center. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several Port St. Lucie locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts. Officials urge drivers to watch for flooded roads, never go around barricades and stay off closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by the flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie allocates $1 million for flood repairs; pre-applications open Thursday
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie has allocated $1 million to help eligible homeowners repair damage from this week's flooding, with pre-applications opening at 8 a.m. Thursday. The city's Disaster Relief Program offers up to $25,000 per eligible homeowner for critical repairs to primary residences. Assistance is limited to low- and moderate-income homeowners and will remain available only until the $1 million allocation is exhausted.

The city announced the allocation Wednesday. Assistance is offered through the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, with funding from the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. Homeowners can receive a 0% interest deferred-payment loan with no monthly payments. The loans are forgiven over five years under program guidelines.

Applicants must meet the program's income requirements and must have owned and occupied their home within Port St. Lucie city limits for at least one year. The home's assessed value must be $560,154 or less. Homeowners also must be current on their mortgage and property tax payments.

The money may cover emergency repairs and other work needed to make a flood-damaged home safe and habitable. Eligible expenses include tree and debris removal needed to restore habitability, payment of homeowners insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. Those repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, and temporary structural stabilization. Other reasonable and necessary actions to protect the home from additional damage may also qualify. All work must be directly connected to the declared disaster and approved by the city before assistance is provided.

The program excludes mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal and remediation. Homeowners whose properties require mold remediation must complete that work before other approved repairs can proceed. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or unpermitted work are also excluded.

Residents can submit pre-applications through the city's housing website beginning Thursday morning. Homeowners seeking help can contact Port St. Lucie's Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, email Housing@cityofpsl.com or visit City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.

“Thank you for your patience and understanding as our community recovers from this unprecedented weather event,” the district said.

cards.headline: David Jolly wins St. Lucie County as turnout rises despite flooding
cards.teaser: Democrat David Jolly received approximately 51% of the county’s vote for governor. Turnout exceeded the 2022 rate despite flooding that forced polling place relocations.
cards.body:
Democrat David Jolly won St. Lucie County in Tuesday’s governor’s race, carrying approximately 51% of the vote to Republican Byron Donalds’ 48% as turnout rose despite flooding that forced last-minute polling place changes. The result marked the first time since 2012 that a Democratic candidate for governor or president won a majority of the county’s vote. Former President Barack Obama carried St. Lucie County with 53.42% that year. Jolly’s county victory came as election officials moved several voting locations because of flooding across Port St. Lucie, Tradition and Fort Pierce.

Voter turnout reached 56.5%, an increase of 5.2 percentage points from the 2022 general election, when 51.3% of registered voters cast ballots. In that election, 122,361 of St. Lucie County’s 238,645 registered voters voted. The county ranked 51st among Florida’s 67 counties, with 16 counties reporting lower turnout. Tuesday’s participation exceeded the county’s previous gubernatorial election turnout rate even as flooding disrupted access to some polling locations and required voters to cast ballots at alternate sites.

St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said the polling place changes were necessary to ensure voters had safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Voters assigned to Oak Hammock K-8 School, Centennial High School and the Paula A. Lewis Library were among those affected by the relocations. Some voters were redirected to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence and Tradition Town Hall. The changes affected several polling places across the three communities as election officials responded to the flooding.

Heavy rainfall submerged roads, stranded vehicles and prompted evacuations across parts of St. Lucie County. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for the county and six other Florida counties. Flooding also forced local public schools to close Tuesday and Wednesday. Those conditions coincided with Election Day, when the county recorded both a higher turnout rate than in 2022 and a Democratic majority in the governor’s race.

According to TCPalm , voter turnout reached 56.5% in the county, up 5.2 percentage points from the 2022 general election , when 51.3% of registered voters cast ballots. Lucie County ranked 51st among Florida's 67 counties, with only 16 counties reporting lower turnout. In 2022, the county had 238,645 registered voters, with 122,361 casting ballots. hero.headline: Florida special session expected to implement Amendment 3 homestead tax relief
hero.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Wednesday that a special legislative session is expected to implement Amendment 3, the voter-approved measure expanding homestead property tax relief. The amendment must be implemented by Jan. 1. DeSantis said the legislation would set a schedule for further relief and seek to prevent local governments from offsetting homeowners’ savings with other taxes or fees.

DeSantis said he would work with legislative leaders to determine when lawmakers should return to Tallahassee before he leaves office in January. He wants lawmakers to establish what he called a “taxpayer bill of rights” and is considering state grants to help local governments cover essential services. That assistance could total tens of millions of dollars, particularly for rural communities facing funding shortfalls for core services such as sheriff’s departments, he said. “It's not going to be a tax shift,” DeSantis said. “It's going to be a reduction.”

Amendment 3 does not apply to school districts, and DeSantis said the implementing legislation would preserve that exemption. He suggested lawmakers could eventually revisit Florida’s education funding formula as they consider additional property tax relief for homeowners without reducing support for public schools. His ultimate goal is to move Florida closer to making homesteaded property tax-free, though he said that would require additional action after his term ends. “The more we can get the homestead to just be tax free, I think that's the better,” he said.

Speaking the day after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, DeSantis also credited Amendment 3 with helping Republicans withstand major Democratic gains elsewhere in the country. He argued that the measure drew voters who then supported Republican candidates further down the ballot. “Had Amendment 3 not been on the ballot, I don't know that we turn out the voters that we ended up turning out,” he said.

DeSantis described the national results as “close to an extinction-level event” for Republicans but said Florida’s results reflected voter trust in the party’s record during his two terms. He urged Republicans nationally to pay greater attention to economic concerns, including inflation, mortgage rates, gas prices, and grocery prices, rather than emphasizing issues he believed had been more effective in earlier elections.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls
cards.body:
Emergency crews handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding in St. Lucie County, officials said Tuesday, as rescue operations continued and the county opened two shelters. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and warned that floodwater could take several days to recede.

Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said crews received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period. County public safety director Ron Guerrero said estimated rainfall totals ranged from 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, areas around California and Peacock boulevards, and areas around Virginia Avenue. The Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Crews were assessing roads and infrastructure. They were also clearing drainage and roadways, though safety concerns limited some high-water operations after dark.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday, Nov. 4, and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, and the landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations.

Officials warned that road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents seeking relocated vehicles can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. The city also warned of a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with pickups shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised avoiding standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and washing with soap and water after exposure. Residents should discard food or household items exposed to floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Flood-affected private wells should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes in Port St. Lucie mayoral race
hero.body:
Steven Giordano unseated Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes Tuesday, with all 62 precincts reporting. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and increasing transparency in city spending.

Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin’s 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Election-day, early and mail votes were marked completely reported as of 12:34 a.m.

During his campaign, Giordano argued that developers should pay their fair share of infrastructure improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as Port St. Lucie continues expanding. He called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion and sought to hold developers accountable for infrastructure improvements. He also called for an independent forensic audit of city spending and promised greater transparency at City Hall.

Martin defended her administration’s approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for a growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard at Savona Boulevard and Tradition Parkway at Village Parkway. Martin also pointed to 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city’s property tax rate.

The candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August’s three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%.

Port St. Lucie voters also rejected a proposal to pay an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly residential garbage collection. The latest election results showed 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The referendum was nonbinding, meaning the vote provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County moving flood shelters as Port St. Lucie flooding persists
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its temporary flood shelters Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen, while significant standing water remains in parts of Port St. Lucie. Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede as recovery efforts continue.

The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter is relocating from the Fenn Center. On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts and working to restore normal conditions safely.

Officials urge residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano defeats Shannon Martin to win Port St. Lucie mayoral race
hero.teaser: Giordano won by just over 2,400 votes, reversing a nearly 13-percentage-point deficit to Martin in the August primary.
hero.body:
Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Shannon Martin by just over 2,400 votes to win the race for Port St. Lucie mayor, reversing his nearly 13-percentage-point deficit in the August primary.

Giordano celebrated with supporters Tuesday night at Recovery Sports Grill in Tradition after pulling ahead with more than 51% of the vote. At his election-night watch party, he said he believed voters responded to his message and approach to the race.

“I think they saw somebody that was dedicated, that was here for all the right reasons,” Giordano said. “I think they watched the debate.”

Giordano said he wants to serve residents rather than approach the position as a politician. “I think they saw somebody who is here for all the right reasons, that's not a politician, that's not here for money, that's here to do the right thing for the people,” he said. “And I'm proud to be the people's mayor.”

The general election followed a contentious August primary that included an FDLE investigation involving campaign signs. The investigation led to Martin's husband and two other Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on paid administrative leave.

hero.headline: Flood-related polling relocations extend beyond Precinct 90 in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Flood-related Election Day polling changes in St. Lucie County extend beyond the relocation of Precinct 90 from Legacy High School to Tradition Town Hall. Election officials also designated replacement voting sites for precincts 49, 71, 51, 67, 86, 83, 92 and 12, with specific access routes for two locations.

The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves were intended to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots.

The notice directs voters in precincts 49 and 71, whose regular polling place is Oak Hammock K-8 School, to the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, are also assigned to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard.

For precincts 67 and 86, the replacement polling place is Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence at 500 NW California Blvd., replacing Centennial High School. The county designates Peacock Boulevard as the access route.

In the Tradition area, Precinct 83 voters are directed from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters, whose regular polling place is The Brennity at Tradition, are also assigned to Tradition Town Hall. That facility is also the replacement site for Precinct 90, where flooding and police roadblocks disrupted access to Legacy High School. The Precinct 90 relocation replaced earlier instructions to reach the school by an alternate route.

In Fort Pierce, the notice directs Precinct 12 voters from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1.

Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin as Port St. Lucie mayor by 2,601 votes
hero.body:
Steven Giordano defeated Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes Tuesday, with all 62 precincts reporting. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements.

Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Election-day, early and mail voting results were marked complete as of 12:34 a.m.

Throughout the campaign, Giordano argued that developers should pay their fair share for infrastructure improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as Port St. Lucie continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion. On city spending, Giordano called for an independent forensic audit and promised greater transparency at City Hall.

Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard at Savona Boulevard and Tradition Parkway at Village Parkway. On taxpayer spending, Martin cited 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate.

The candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%.

Port St. Lucie voters also rejected a proposal to pay an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly residential garbage collection. The results showed 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The nonbinding referendum provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

We didn’t anticipate anything like what transpired yesterday. Caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry, Prince said. Schools are closed Wednesday. Prince said the district expects to reopen Thursday if roads are clear, and that no school buildings took significant water. A private security company that patrols homeowners associations in the Tradition area joined the rescue effort with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. We had no goal when we came out here. We had just ambition to figure out how we can help anyone and anywhere and do whatever we can with the resources that we have, Matchton said. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods, and warned that anyone who preys on flood victims will face zero tolerance. The sheriff said there was no playbook for a storm like this. But the most important thing is we’re all working together with one purpose, which is to serve this community, Del Toro said. The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals, and coffee. Anybody who may need a place tonight, please come in, Lamb said. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. County leaders said it could take up to seven days for conditions to return to normal. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials ask residents to stay home if they can and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov .

cards.headline: Fort Pierce restaurant owner promotes free books, renovates space for reading room
cards.teaser: Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is helping children get books mailed to their homes through New Worlds Reading while turning part of his restaurant into a reading room.
cards.body:
FORT PIERCE, Fla. Scott Van Duzer, owner of Big Apple Pizza, is working to connect children with free books mailed to their homes while renovating part of his restaurant into a reading room. He wants to expand access to books for children, especially those from low-income families.

Van Duzer has been involved with Read To Succeed, which he said has distributed 40,000 books over three years. He is now promoting New Worlds Reading as a way to get books to children more quickly. Van Duzer said signing up takes less than five minutes and children receive nine free books a year through fifth grade.

Amy York and her son Tripp read together using books he receives through New Worlds Reading. York described the program as a partnership with the University of Florida and Scholastic. “Well, it's awesome because they ship the books right to your house,” York said.

The reading room renovation is another part of Van Duzer’s effort to help children improve their reading. He emphasized the importance of giving children access to books early and keeping books in their homes. “It's just essential that we get books in kids' hands earlier and to have them in the home,” he said.

hero.headline: Angie Nixon concedes Florida U.S. Senate special election to Ashley Moody
hero.body:
Democrat Angie Nixon conceded Florida’s U.S. Senate special election Tuesday after Republican Sen. Ashley Moody was projected to win, with votes still being counted.

Moody had just over 50% of the vote to Nixon’s approximately 48% as counting continued. Nixon, a Jacksonville Democrat and Florida state representative, had sought to become the state’s first Black U.S. senator.

In her concession speech, Nixon told supporters she would continue fighting for her progressive agenda. “We may have lost this battle, but the war is not over,” she said.

Nixon entered the general election after a surprise victory in the Democratic primary. Her campaign focused on affordability, with proposals including Medicare for All, free child care and rent freezes. Some supporters viewed the relatively close race as an opportunity for Democrats in a state where Republicans have built a substantial advantage.

Supporter Mak Manning praised Nixon’s grassroots campaign. “She's willing to get out there and into the streets and fight,” Manning said.

Nixon identified fundraising and closing the voter registration gap with Republicans as challenges facing Democrats. “That 1.5 million gap in registration, we need to fix that,” she said.

Asked about her next steps, Nixon said her immediate plans included getting some sleep. She also looked toward another election cycle: “I’m looking forward to 2028 because we’re getting to work,” she said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 flood rescues and water-related calls; schools closed Wednesday
hero.body:
St. Lucie County emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding, county officials said Tuesday. Schools were set to remain closed Wednesday, with two shelters open and officials urging residents to avoid unnecessary travel as crews continued rescues and assessed roads.

Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said the fire district received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period. County Public Safety Director Ron Guerrero said estimated rainfall totals ranged from 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards, as well as Virginia Avenue.

The county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Crews were assessing roads and infrastructure while clearing drainage and roadways, Guerrero said. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria urged caution and said water could take several days to recede.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. Guerrero said about 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the briefing. The school district hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, and the landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations.

Officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents seeking relocated vehicles can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. Solid waste collection was expected to run one day late, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and evacuated neighborhoods.

Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised avoiding standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and washing with soap and water after exposure. Food and household items exposed to floodwater should not be used. Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. Guerrero said the county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Officials were continuing high-water rescues, assessing roads and infrastructure, and working with public works crews to clear drainage and roadways. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the county landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. He said the district had not seen significant water intrusion in its schools but would assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Lucie officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Officials urge residents to avoid floodwater Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and neighborhoods that had been evacuated. He warned against taking advantage of residents affected by flooding and said the Sheriff’s Office would take those cases seriously. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. hero.headline: Flooding forces polling place moves in Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie for Election Day
hero.body:
Flooding and unsafe road conditions forced temporary polling place relocations in Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie for Tuesday’s election. St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker announced the changes Monday to give voters safe, accessible places to cast their ballots.

Election officials urged voters to verify their assigned polling locations before leaving home because additional changes may be necessary as flooding conditions evolve. Voters can check www.stlucievotes.gov or call the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 for updates.

The announced changes are:

• Precinct 12: Voting moved from Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to Days Inn Midtown, the Precinct 25 location, at 3224 S. 1, Fort Pierce, FL 34982.

• Precincts 49 and 71: Voting moved from Oak Hammock K-8 School to Port St. Lucie Community Center, the Precinct 45 location, at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Precinct 51: Voting moved from Disabled American Veterans Hall to Port St. Lucie Community Center, the Precinct 45 location, at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Lucie West Centennial High School: Voting moved to Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence at 500 NW California Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34986. Access is from Peacock Boulevard.

• Lewis Library: Voting moved to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

• Precinct 92: Voting moved from The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

The relocations followed days of heavy rainfall that flooded roads. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of widespread flooding and threats to public safety and infrastructure.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways.

hero.headline: Rick Meltzer wins open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat
hero.body:
Rick Meltzer won the open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat, succeeding three-term Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan after campaigning on infrastructure-first growth and tighter spending oversight. With 58 of 62 precincts reporting, Meltzer had 56.7 percent of the vote to Idony Jean Baptist’s 43.3 percent. The district covers the city’s eastern and northeastern areas. Morgan did not seek reelection.

Meltzer, a mortgage loan originator and political newcomer, has lived in District 1 for more than 20 years. He has spent 17 years coaching and mentoring in youth sports. He says he would bring an outsider’s perspective to City Hall, with a platform focused on affordability, accountability and infrastructure. Meltzer led the four-candidate August primary with about 42 percent of the vote, followed by his opponent at about 22 percent. Neither reached the majority needed to win outright.

Meltzer says he would seek budget cuts and lower property taxes while holding contractors and developers to project deadlines and budgets. He wants road, utility and other infrastructure needs addressed before the city approves new development. He also opposes more zero-lot-line housing and supports building a sports complex. Meltzer has said he is researching the impacts of data centers, including water use, electricity demand and noise. He says their potential tax revenue and jobs could outweigh those concerns if the city protects residents’ interests.

Idony Jean Baptist is a minister and former Indian River County Sheriff’s Office detention deputy who ran for the same council seat in 2022 and later briefly filed to run for St. Lucie County sheriff before withdrawing. His campaign emphasized safer communities, transparent government, listening to residents, helping people in need and supporting small businesses. He proposed attracting more businesses to grow city revenue and reduce service costs for residents. He also supported moving to a double-can automated trash-pickup system, which he said could improve service and save money.

Jean Baptiste is a minister and former Indian River County Sheriff’s Office detention deputy. cards.headline: Troy Ingersoll wins sixth term on St. Lucie County School Board, defeating Lisa Kessler
cards.teaser: The School Board chairman won the District 5 runoff after Lisa Kessler narrowly led the August primary. Ingersoll identifies teacher staffing and rapid population growth as major challenges for the district.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County School Board Chairman Troy Ingersoll has secured a sixth term, defeating political newcomer Lisa Kessler in the District 5 runoff after a closely divided August primary. Ingersoll, who has served on the board since 2006, returns with priorities that include safe schools, stronger student achievement and responsible budgeting. He identifies teacher recruitment and retention, rapid population growth and leadership development as major challenges for the district’s next term.

Kessler narrowly led the August primary with 37.5% of the vote, compared with Ingersoll’s 37.2%, a difference of 167 votes. Charles Cerami received 25.2%. District 5 covers the eastern, coastal portion of the school district. School Board candidates must live in the districts they seek to represent, but all registered St. Lucie County voters were eligible to cast ballots in the nonpartisan race.

Ingersoll supports maintaining accelerated academic programs through consistent funding, targeted interventions and teacher development. He owns Pinch A Penny Pools and Spas in Vero Beach and serves as pastor of Midway Road Baptist Church. He holds a criminology degree from Florida State University and a master’s degree from New Orleans Baptist Theological Seminary.

Kessler campaigned on academic standards in reading, math, science and career readiness, along with recruiting and retaining qualified teachers. Her platform also emphasized stronger career and technical education, arts programs, better communication between schools and families, transparent budgeting and treating parents as partners in school decisions. She says public schools should make their case to families by highlighting certified teachers and programs unavailable elsewhere. A small-business owner, bestselling author and chair of the Fort Pierce Arts and Culture Advisory Board, Kessler spent 26 years in sales and marketing management before writing full time. Her campaign also highlighted her background as the daughter of two lifelong public-school teachers and her 11 years as a Girl Scout troop leader.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 rescues and water-related calls; schools closed Wednesday
hero.body:
Emergency crews in St. Lucie County had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding Tuesday, officials said. Schools will remain closed Wednesday, Nov. 4. Crews continued rescue operations, assessed roads and infrastructure, and worked to clear drainage and roadways. Public Safety Director Ron Guerrero said some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying at the shelters at the time of the county briefing, Guerrero said. Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and said water could take several days to recede.

Guerrero said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition and neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive. It also affected areas around California and Peacock boulevards, as well as Virginia Avenue. Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said the fire district received 518 calls for service over 36 hours. The county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation.

The school district hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check Port St. Lucie’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. The city also warned of a one-day solid waste collection delay, with collection shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. Residents should avoid standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and wash with soap and water after exposure. Food and household items that touched floodwater should not be eaten or used. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water, boil tap water or disinfect it. Flood-affected private wells should be tested for bacteria before use resumes. Questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can be directed to 772-873-4931.

hero.headline: Roberts wins reelection to Martin County School Board District 1 with 60.14%
hero.body:
Christia Li Roberts won reelection to the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat with 60.14% of the vote, defeating Cherie White, who received 39.86%. The nonpartisan contest returned the 12-year incumbent to the board. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. Its schools and facilities include Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center.

Roberts’ priorities include preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028. She says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. Her campaign emphasized academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management. Roberts pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has generated additional operating revenue for schools. She also wants to improve student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction. Her goals include expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs.

A Stuart resident, Roberts has served on the School Board since 2014. She is a registered investment adviser and financial consultant with a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, she was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization supporting school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69%, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%.

White, a Jensen Beach resident, campaigned on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. White identified employee retention as an early priority, calling for fair pay, supportive work environments and stronger recruitment. She also proposed more campus-level decision-making, additional support for disadvantaged students and a plain-language budget with charts and visual data to help residents understand district spending.

Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

hero.headline: Brian Mast wins reelection in Florida's 21st Congressional District
hero.body:
Republican Brian Mast won reelection Tuesday in Florida's 21st Congressional District, defeating Democratic challenger James Martin and securing another two-year term in the U.S. House of Representatives. The newly redrawn district includes portions of Palm Beach, Martin and St. Lucie counties.

Mast has served in Congress since 2017 and chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Before entering politics, he served in the U.S. Army, losing both legs while serving in Afghanistan.

Martin, a U.S. Coast Guard veteran and former national security official in the Biden administration, won the Democratic primary in August. The general election field also included no-party-affiliation candidate Alexander Cooke and write-in candidate David Fabrikant.

hero.headline: Martin County schools weigh Wednesday operations after Tuesday flooding closure
hero.body:
The Martin County School District is evaluating weather-related damage and safety conditions before deciding whether classes will resume Wednesday, Nov. 4, following a Tuesday closure caused by severe flooding. Schools were closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, as flooding affected the Treasure Coast. The district said it would announce its Wednesday plans as soon as it finishes reviewing conditions. In its message, the district acknowledged that families and employees need to make arrangements around the school schedule. It said protecting students, staff and families remains its main concern as it determines whether schools can operate safely. The assessment will guide the district’s decision on Wednesday operations.

In neighboring St. Lucie County, school officials have announced that schools will remain closed Wednesday. Superintendent Dr. Prince announced the closure Tuesday after the district coordinated with local law enforcement and consulted the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district expects schools to reopen Thursday, Nov. 5. Beyond the school closure, the district is helping with the response to flooding in the community. School resource officers are assisting with efforts on local roads, and a shelter has opened at one of the district’s school sites for families who have been displaced because their homes flooded.

Indian River County Public Schools and district locations will also stay closed Wednesday, Nov. 4, because flooded roads continue to make travel unsafe. Officials said assessments found district facilities operational, but transportation conditions remain a barrier to reopening. With 31 roads closed, school buses cannot run safely. The district hopes to reopen Thursday, Nov. Officials said they will continue coordinating with emergency management as they work toward reopening. Families and employees will receive updates through the district’s social media accounts and Live Feed as plans are confirmed. The Wednesday closure applies to both schools and district locations.

Okeechobee County schools, meanwhile, will reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, the district announced. The reopening follows work by crews to ensure schools and bus stops were safe and ready for students after the weather event. In announcing the return, the district thanked families and the broader community for their patience during those preparations. It also recognized the work of its operations, maintenance and custodial teams, along with school administrators and Okeechobee County Emergency Management. Okeechobee’s announcement confirms a Wednesday return, while Martin County continues its assessment and St. Lucie and Indian River counties keep schools closed that day.

A crash involving a loaded cement truck is causing road closures on 84th Avenue north of SW Martin Highway in Martin County, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office.

The truck went off the roadway and rolled over in a ditch. The Sheriff’s Office described the incident as a single-vehicle crash.

No injuries were reported in the crash, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency is investigating.

Significant delays are expected while crews work to remove the truck, the Sheriff’s Office said.

hero.headline: Election Day flooding disrupts access to Legacy High School in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
Flooding disrupted access to Legacy High School in Port St. Lucie on Tuesday, creating confusion for Precinct 90 voters as residents voted for the city’s next mayor. Voters assigned to the high school were being redirected to Precinct 89 at Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane in Port St. Lucie. The change followed travel problems around the school, where flooding and police roadblocks had affected access earlier in the day. The updated direction for Precinct 90 voters was to go to Tradition Town Hall rather than continue to Legacy High School.

Earlier Tuesday, the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections had instructed voters to reach Legacy High School by taking Midway Road and Glade Extension. Flooding and roadblocks on Southwest Village Parkway prevented access from that direction, and police had closed that entrance to the campus. An alternate route initially allowed voters to reach the school despite the closure. The instructions changed from using another route to the high school to voting at a different location. Tradition Town Hall was also listed as the polling location for Precinct 92, which previously voted at The Brennity at Tradition.

Other polling location changes in St. Lucie County included Precinct 12, whose voters were directed to Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S. Highway 1 in Fort Pierce instead of the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge. Voters in Precincts 49 and 71 were assigned to the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., replacing Oak Hammock K-8 School. Precinct 51 voters were also assigned to the community center, replacing the Disabled American Veterans Hall. Voters going to the community center were instructed to enter from Airoso Boulevard. The center was listed as the voting site for all three precincts.

The MIDFLORIDA Credit Union Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place in Port St. Lucie, was listed as the voting location for Precincts 67 and 86. It was also the location for Precincts 85 and 95, which previously voted at the Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence. Voters in Precincts 6 and 28 were directed to the Havert L. Fenn Center at 2000 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce. Their previous polling location was Renaissance Business Park, formerly known as Orange Blossom Business Center. Paula A. Lewis Library remained open as a polling location.

hero.headline: Flooding forces Election Day polling-place moves in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Flooding has prompted Election Day polling-place changes in St. Lucie County, with affected voters directed to alternate locations in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites.

The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. The office said the moves are intended to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots.

In Port St. Lucie, voters in precincts 49 and 71, who normally vote at Oak Hammock K-8 School, will vote at the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, whose usual polling place is the Disabled American Veterans Hall, will also vote at the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard.

Voters in precincts 67 and 86 will move from Centennial High School to Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence at 500 NW California Blvd. The county says access is from Peacock Boulevard.

In the Tradition area, precinct 83 voters will move from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters, who normally vote at The Brennity at Tradition, will also vote at Tradition Town Hall.

In Fort Pierce, Precinct 12 voters will move from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1.

Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov.

cards.headline: Flooding prompts Tuesday closures of St. Lucie County schools, offices and courthouses
cards.teaser: Officials urge residents to travel only when necessary as numerous roads are flooded or impassable. Deputies and emergency personnel are coordinating with the Emergency Operations Center.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County public schools, county government offices and courthouses will be closed Tuesday as significant rainfall and flooding affect the area. County officials are urging residents to stay off the roads unless travel is necessary. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of widespread flooding and threats to public safety and critical infrastructure.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said numerous roads are flooded or impassable, with more rain expected through Monday night and Tuesday. The agency urged residents to stay home, never drive through floodwaters and avoid moving or driving around barricades and road-closure signs. Residents should stay away from downed power lines and standing water near electrical equipment, and monitor official sources for weather alerts and road updates. Deputies and other personnel remain on duty and are coordinating with the Emergency Operations Center. The sheriff’s office thanked deputies, dispatchers, emergency personnel and community partners responding to the conditions and urged residents to look out for their neighbors.

Flooding also has affected road access to some polling locations, prompting the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections to announce temporary polling-place changes for the Nov. 3 General Election. Voters in Precinct 12, whose usual polling place is Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge, should go to Days Inn Midtown. Voters in Precincts 49 and 71, originally at Oak Hammock K-8 School, and Precinct 51, originally at Disabled American Veterans Hall, should go to Port St. Lucie Community Center, 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

Voters in Precincts 67 and 86, originally at St. Lucie West Centennial High School, should go to Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence, 500 NW California Blvd., with access from Peacock Boulevard. Voters in Precinct 83, originally at Paula A. Lewis Library, and Precinct 92, originally at The Brennity at Tradition, should go to Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane. More information about voting and vote-by-mail ballots is available at stlucievotes.gov or by calling the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500.

hero.headline: Indian River County declares flooding emergency; Rockridge under voluntary evacuation
hero.body:
Indian River County is under a local state of emergency because of flooding, and a voluntary evacuation order is in effect for the Rockridge neighborhood due to flooding and potential wastewater backups, county officials announced Monday, Nov. 2.

The emergency took effect at 2:30 p.m. Monday and will remain in effect until further notice. The county government cited deteriorating weather conditions, numerous roadways made impassable by flooding and continuing rainfall throughout Indian River County.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced the voluntary evacuation Monday night for Rockridge, from 17th Street to 13th Place and 6th Avenue to IR BLVD. Indian River County Utilities is monitoring conditions and has contacted affected customers. Residents with questions or who want to report their status should call 772-226-4000, the sheriff's office said.

hero.headline: Martin County schools assess flooding as Wednesday reopening decision remains pending
hero.body:
The Martin County School District is assessing flooding impacts and travel safety before deciding whether schools will reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, following Tuesday’s closure. The Wednesday decision remains pending as the district reviews conditions after severe flooding along the Treasure Coast.

The district said it will announce Wednesday’s schedule as soon as possible after completing its assessment. It acknowledged that families and employees are making plans and said the safety and well-being of students, staff and families remain its priority. Martin County schools closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, because of flooding.

The St. Lucie County School District announced Tuesday that its schools will remain closed Wednesday. The decision was made in collaboration with local law enforcement and in consultation with the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district anticipates reopening Thursday, Nov. 5. School resource officers are supporting efforts on local roadways, and the district has opened a shelter at one of its school sites for families displaced by flooded homes.

Indian River County Public Schools and district locations also will remain closed Wednesday because flooding continues to make travel unsafe. Officials said district facilities have been assessed and are operational, but 31 roads are closed and conditions prevent school buses from operating safely. The district hopes to reopen Thursday, Nov. 5, and continues to work with emergency management officials. It will share updates through its social media channels and Live Feed as reopening plans are confirmed.
